To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. Specifically, we explore the possibility that magnetic fields with limits of 4-8 EeV and a rapid cut-off above 8 EeV, coupled with an energy-dependent composition, could account for our observations. We also consider the likelihood that our detection represents a temporary pattern, given its duration and energy scale, and suggest the necessity for further research prompted by our analysis. Despite difficulties posed by statistical thresholds and detector domains, we believe that a thorough analysis of anisotropy at extremely energetic levels will contribute substantially to the understanding of cosmic rays and their origins. Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal nulls in a 36GHz bandwidth, severely hindering BER performance. To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer was initially applied with satisfactory results, however its effectiveness was impeded due to the occurrence of burst errors resulting from unpredictable marine conditions. To mitigate this issue, a weighted DFE method was developed but proved insufficient as it was unable to fully compensate for the spectral distortions due to the limited scope of its feedback symbols. Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. We've demonstrated the efficacy of this approach on diverse time-series datasets on two tasks: time-series classification and forecasting. Our findings indicate a substantial reduction in parameter count, increased model flexibility, and improved robustness to dataset variations. The technique is adaptable and can be applied to other convolutional networks. The source code is publicly available, and the optimized models for the discussed datasets can be accessed through a model hub. By addressing the dilation factor challenge, we intend to accelerate the adoption of efficient TCNs for complex, real-world time-series applications.

This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation and contrast it with existing data repair approaches. We demonstrate the practical applicability of our method through a customizable tool, available online. This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. The results of our analysis have provided valuable insights into time series forecasting and have demonstrated the TV-PARX model's effectiveness in identifying complex patterns and shifts within data sets. Consequently, we have produced accurate and robust forecasting outcomes that can be utilized in various applications requiring prediction of count-based time series data. Our research implementation is complemented by a suitable R function for estimation and forecasting utilizing the `tvparx` package. This implementation is further illustrated by an example involving COVID-19 forecasts. We performed the first in-depth analysis of seven red giant members in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. We used the APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra to examine the abundance levels of multiple chemical species in these stars. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/ChenBerry/Object-Pose-Refined. Visualizing the likelihood distribution of projected corners can provide valuable insights and is openly shared at https://object-pose-refined.github.io/. 

Keywords: Object Pose Estimation, Two-Stage Pipelines, Correspondence Learning, Projection grouping, Convolutional Neural Networks. 

This work has been accepted for oral presentation at the 13th Asian Conference on Computer Vision (ACCV 2020).

We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address General Graphical Lasso
challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), Graphical Lasso
estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced by Dempster (1972)
under Covariance Selection. The framework has been expanded to accommodate
hidden variables in Chandrasekaran (2012) and can jointly estimate multiple
inverse covariance matrices, as shown in Danaher (2013) and Tomasi (2018). The
GGLasso package supports the resolution of diverse formulations and notable
subcases like Graphical Lasso with latent variables, Group, and Fused Graphical Lasso. Moreover, it
includes an efficient matrix representation for simultaneous covariance matrix
estimation and a useful utility tool to evaluate BIC for graphical models. The
library is highly flexible and user-friendly, making it easy to model complex
situations and compare different models by conducting a non-sparsified analysis.

Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. Unlike current hybrid algorithms that may become trapped in local minima, our proposed algorithm uses a more efficient approach to solve these equations, allowing for a higher probability of reaching the optimal solution. Through simulations and real-world applications, our method demonstrates greater accuracy and efficiency when compared to other multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks. Specifically, our approach was effective in identifying key nodes in a social network, a network focusing on collaborative behavior, and a network related to topic identification. Notably, our method has a practical application in indentifying influential spreaders that can disrupt the dissemination of malicious information in a network by providing accurate results in a reasonable amount of time. We tackle the issue of non-blind deblurring and demosaicking on noisy raw images using a learning-based approach tailored to handle these images directly, with an innovative new component that simultaneously demosaicks and deblurs them in an interpretable way. To train this model, we utilize real-world camera data transformed into raw images through a realistic process, mimicking real-world camera functions. By doing so, we demonstrate the advantages of our single-stage model over traditional approaches combining demosaicking and deblurring modules, according to objective performance metrics. Additionally, our method is capable of removing a camera's intrinsic blurring effect, which effectively enables deblurring of sharper images from actual pictures. Experimental results show that our proposed model surpasses state-of-the-art methods in both objective and subjective evaluations on real-world images. Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Fock coordinate transformation. This transformation 
corresponds to a de Sitter spacetime. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation within 
$R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish that it is analogous to the Dirac equation defined 
within the de Sitter spacetime, described by its conformally flat metric. We then propose 
a novel strategy to solve the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime by adopting 
the Schr\"{o}dinger picture. This involves utilizing the deformed Poisson brackets to derive 
a set of first-order differential equations. We can then obtain the precise expression 
for the Dirac current within the de Sitter spacetime by applying Noether's technique. 
We also establish that the proposed solution for the Dirac equation within the de Sitter 
spacetime can be obtained through a specific non-complex transformation of the solutions 
derived for the Schr\"{o}dinger picture. This non-complex transformation appears to be an 
extension of the well-known Wick transformation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the 
divergence of the Dirac current within the de Sitter spacetime is negative and may be 
related to the negative mass cosmological constant. This result is obtained without 
utilizing the Wick transformation. We propose that this approach can be applied to 
other spin systems, such as the Klein-Gordon equation. We also suggest that this approach 
can be employed to analyze the behavior of particle systems in the context of curved spacetime. 
We conclude by highlighting the potential for this approach to be used in the study 
of condensed matter systems, where the spacetime curvature is significant.

picture, Noether's technique, Dirac current, convergence.

This often misplaced trust is the foundation on which our objective is built – namely to minimize the reliance on device hardware and software components for users to withstand cyber threats. 

We introduce an innovative multi-domain hardware setup consisting of isolated sections, where programs are partitioned statically to prevent malicious interaction. 

A few key hardware components with proven security functionality are integrated to grant secure temporary access to processing resources and external input/output interfaces simultaneously.

To manage these hardware components, we introduce OctopOS, a unique OS comprising several secure subsystems working together in distrust. 

We showcase a functioning prototype, incorporating our hardware and software, utilizing a combined CPU-FPGA board with an acceptable additional hardware expense in comparison to existing SoCs.

Finally, we outline possible pathways for further optimizing performance and integrating more intricate security mechanisms.

Problems of control, estimation, and system design can be redefined as optimization problems subject to specific constraints. However, given the infinite dimensionality of these issues, it becomes necessary to employ numerical techniques to approximate a solution. We explore specific methods used in simultaneous direct approaches, specifically the transcription process. Our focus is on collocation, residual integration, and Runge-Kutta schemes, highlighting their applications to a case study related to the ventilator shortage during the COVID-19 pandemic. Our study investigated the possibility of ventilating more than one patient on a single ventilator by estimating patient parameters with a limited number of flow rate measurements, modifying air flow resistance, and controlling the ventilator's pressure to ensure desired tidal volumes for both patients. Furthermore, our findings underscore the importance of optimizing solution approximations through a well-designed global search. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these sites frequently contain complex hydrocarbon reservoirs. Achieving optimal well placement and reducing costs necessitates real-time geosteering. This process is usually supported by up-to-date formation evaluations derived from the interpretation of well logs acquired during drilling. For this application, a reliable, fast, and robust approach to well-log interpretation in real-time is essential to capture the associated uncertainties. We incorporated an ensemble-based iterative method called LM-EnRML, a computationally efficient form of the Levenberg Marquardt method within our formation evaluation framework. This method determines parameters such as resistivity, density, and boundary locations along with their uncertainties by minimizing discrepancies between the measured well logging data and simulated results. Several synthetic scenarios with diverse logs confirmed that this method can yield accurate parameter estimations. The comparison of computational times indicated that LM-EnRML possesses at least 10 to 125 times faster CPU times relative to conventional methods such as Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo, while the ensemble-based approach allows for concurrent processing on multiple CPUs. The successful testing of the proposed method in a simulated case mimicking real field data demonstrated precise formation evaluations, demonstrating that LM-EnRML is an efficient and reliable method to calculate petrophysical formation properties, layer boundaries, and related uncertainties making it suitable for real-time geosteering. However, the method's ability to perform safely and efficiently relies on the correctness of the modeling equations, parameter initialization, and boundary conditions. Therefore, this algorithm can be used in real-time applications, such as geosteering, where the model equations and initialization techniques are well-established and highly reliable. Additionally, this method can be applied in other problems solving non-linear, direct optimization problems by minimizing differences between measured data and simulated results. In addition to well logging, this approach can be used to solve other direct optimization problems involving different types of data. Ultimately, this method can be used in any problem that involves the calculation of parameters, where the model equations are differentiable, and the parameters can be initialized correctly. This includes well logging, well placement, history matching in reservoir simulation, imaging of seismic data, optical parameter estimation, magnetic field modeling, and chemical kinetics parameter estimation. This method has several advantages over conventional methods such as Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo, due to its safety, robustness, and computational efficiency. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability from sentence-level to corpus-level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvement in domain adaptation through the proposed holistic modeling. Additionally, our evaluations reveal improved robustness with the incorporation of corpus-level information, leading to superior performance when compared to non-adaptive models. Research into the location detection of mobile nodes within wireless sensor networks is currently ongoing. We develop and test an innovative RSSI-based location finding method suitable for 802.15.4 (ZigBee) networks. To counteract interference between different technologies operating in the same frequency range, we design and execute a new method for calculating the distance between nodes. The aim of this approach is to minimize the average error in location estimation, and when compared to ideal, interference-free results, we have achieved a level of accuracy of less than half a metre using actual hardware. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of using this new method in conjunction with the ZigBee network's data transmission process. We observe that implementing this location detection method causes a significant delay, however, it does not have a substantial impact on the network's overall location determination process. To enhance the algorithm's effectiveness across different scenarios, we outline a potential direction for optimization. The testing was conducted using a setup consisting of 16 sensor nodes and a mobile node, with the algorithm being tested under both indoor and best-case (minimum interference) scenarios. Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, models, and resources to enhance NLP applications for societal betterment, exemplified through an analysis of code-mixing between English and Hindi but with implications for other language combinations. By leveraging the unique characteristics of code-mixing, researchers can create more sophisticated models that adapt across languages, enabling more effective NLP for a broader spectrum of multilingual communities. 

This work has been inspired by the Workshop on Multilingual NLP at the 2020 Conference of the Association for Computational Linguistics, and the authors hope that the issued raised will benefit the broader NLP community, contributing to greater diversity, inclusivity, and accessibility in NLP through code-mixing. This paper's objectives are threefold: (1) introduce fundamental concepts and challenges in multilingual NLP, specifically code-mixing, before exploring potential applications in crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech; (2) examine current datasets and models in multilingual NLP, code-mixing, and the identified domains, as well as discuss obstacles hindering further progress; (3) outline potential future directions through newly proposed datasets, models, and resources, with initial experiments demonstrating their efficacy. Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives. For instance, we could utilize human descriptions to these images, obtained through crowd sourcing, with the advantage of being relatively low-cost. Moreover, such data has additional benefits, such as enabling the development of preference models that can predict how users will rate description-quality, based on visual features, user demographics, and interaction history. This paper introduces novel evaluation metrics for automatic image description systems, incorporating both perceptual features and user-specific factors, which can enhance the transparency of scoring, making it easier to compare our proposed approach with other description generation methods. Experiments with both simple and complex scoring mechanisms demonstrate the benefits of these new metrics, leading to consistent performance improvements, and notable gains with datasets that have low-quality reference data. Notably, our proposed approach proves particularly effective with the larger, more diverse test sets, highlighting the potential for its application in real-world scenarios. The code and data developed as part of this research are now available online, along with comprehensive instructions for replicating its results. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. However, only populations living in areas where politics are highly divided experienced increased dissemination of partisan news and misinformation. These findings have implications for the targeting and effectiveness of misinformation combat strategies on social media. They suggest that although population density plays a key role in misinformation dissemination, there are underlying causes that preexist and contribute to the spread of misinformation. Therefore, simply removing users with high misinformation engagement from social media may have limited effectiveness in reducing the problem's root causes. Instead, designers of online platforms should focus on developing targeted measures that take into account the cultural and political characteristics of various user communities. Moreover, combating misinformation requires a multi-faceted approach that goes beyond technical solutions and involves collaboration with scholars and researchers to understand the underlying causes of the problem. We also tested the validity of our model using alternative datasets and assessed the influence of various online communities' characteristics, such as user bio data and engagement patterns, which showed limited impact on misinformation dissemination. We conclude that the physical and cultural segmentation of the American people contributes significantly to the dissemination of misinformation, and urge researchers to explore more holistic theories that take account of these factors. We introduce a groundbreaking, efficient, and user-friendly detection algorithm called HALFADO. HALFADO uses a limited number of human judgments to effectively identify anomalies in real-time, high-frequency data streams. Implementing a precise detection system is crucial for empowering human teams across the digital world by providing reliable decision support. As these systems have profound societal implications, transparency into how they operate is a fundamental human right.

Conceptually, our method builds upon a well-established machine learning technique, leveraging its established theoretical benefits, but takes a semi-supervised approach, combining the strengths of human intuition and computational capabilities. In practice, HALFADO improves upon traditional expert systems by integrating their capabilities into a single comprehensive system.

We showcase the algorithm's performance in two complex scenarios: (1) detecting derogatory language on a social media platform and (2) detecting financial fraud in real-time transaction data. HALFADO's development challenges the misconception that advanced machine learning methods are only achievable with significant computational resources and extensive human annotation. The code for HALFADO is openly available, providing a versatile detection framework that is adaptable to various applications and data streams. Furthermore, we highlight potential pathways for enhancing the algorithm in response to evolving digital challenges.

Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. Furthermore, our findings suggest that speech content is relatively consistent across different vocabulary options available to humans, which may be a beneficial area for further exploration in future research. By recognizing the significance of this auditory feedback, we can work towards developing more effective robotic learning algorithms that make the most of spoken instructions and feedback from their instructors. This paves the way for robotic systems to safely operate in environments where they are trained by humans in the presence of other people, who may provide verbal feedback throughout the process. This research provides a crucial foundation for exploring the complex interactions between speech patterns and the underlying content that drives them, which involves a multidisciplinary approach combining computer science, robotics, and linguistics. To facilitate further research, we are sharing our dataset of human instructions to the Sawyer robot, which is available for download and is characterized by a range of speech patterns and underlying structures. This dataset is accompanied by a thorough analysis of the spectral tone variation and other related features, which is also included in the accompanying paper that is available for download as well. This research is part of a larger effort to enhance robotic learning through demonstration-based methods that can accommodate and value the input from human teachers. A promising approach to address this difficulty is through the study of conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, specifically focusing on the universal sector of the energy-momentum tensor in this context. A key unifying framework consists of Euler-Arnold equations and their broader integro-differential generalizations, ensuring the well-posedness of state or operator complexity optimization problems. Our comprehensive investigation extends upon our prior findings in arXiv:2005.02415, delving into intricate details of employed methodologies. A notable discussion involves differential regularization strategies, solving the integro-differential equation for Fubini-Study state complexity, and further exploring the underlying geometric properties. Additionally, our research introduces operator complexity dimensions as state complexity's natural extension, accompanied by an in-depth analysis of its fundamental characteristics. Our study also introduces the concept of universal density matrices, formally defined by optimizing a minimum norm under fixed Fubini-Study state complexity, and offers theoretical density matrix examples. Our work also finds the complexity of harmonic maps, a well-known solution to Euler-Arnold equations, resulting in novel formulas for state or operator complexity in the form of elliptic integrals. We have also discovered the relationship between operator complexity dimensions and harmonic map geodesic depth, also explicitly calculating the state complexity of Fubini-Study states for various universal conformal field theories. Our research also establishes the connection between operator complexity and entanglement thickness, both at an instant and over time, offering our first theoretical definition of entanglement complexity and exploring its fundamental characteristics. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. Despite these challenges, we have made progress in applying classic software testing techniques to conversational systems, and are exploring novel methods to address unique challenges posed by systems that can both understand and generate natural language. We offer our research as a foundation for further discussion and improvement of the quality of conversational systems. Despite the existing limitations, we have achieved notable results with our testing framework, and are confident that our approach can serve as a starting point for advancing the field. Previous studies have demonstrated that Translation Memory (TM) can enhance Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance. Unlike existing approaches which rely on bilingual corpora for TM and employ source-side similarity searches, our proposed framework leverages monolingual data and retrieves memories in a cross-lingual manner. Notably, our framework offers two significant advantages: firstly, it enables vast amounts of monolingual data to be incorporated into TM; secondly, both the memory retriever and the NMT model can be jointly optimized for translation objectives. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves substantial gains in performance and outperforms TM-augmented NMT baselines even when utilizing bilingual TM. Furthermore, our model's capacity to tap into monolingual data allows it to excel in low-resource and domain adaptation scenarios. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ghrua/XLM-TM.

Researchers have suggested that specific patterns in the Cosmic Microwave Background, namely low-variance circles and Hawking points, could provide evidence for the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model. These patterns are predicted to originate from previous black hole mergers and evaporation events. We analyzed the Planck and WMAP data using a machine learning tool called HawkingNet, and initially found potential anomalies resembling low-variance circles and Hawking points. However, these anomalies were later removed, and upon re-examination, we found no statistically significant evidence supporting the existence of low-variance circles or Hawking points. Our analysis does indicate the presence of local non-Gaussian fluctuations in the CMB, suggesting that the real sky may differ from theoretical predictions. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. The holistic approach of MSDCR facilitates concurrent improvement in recommendation accuracy across each participating domain, a notable advantage over conventional CDR methods that typically prioritize the target domain at the expense of others. Moreover, the concise and efficient architecture of MSDCR, devoid of intricate interactions between domains, enables seamless scalability to increasing numbers of participating domains. As a result, MSDCR emerges as an exemplary multi-target CDR framework tailored for numerous data-poor domains. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/hongzheng1993/MSDCR.

The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. Building upon this finding, we propose that this strategic coordination could serve as a foundation for developing models of collective behavior in dynamical systems. Furthermore, we suggest that the features observed in our model may be relevant to understanding the emergence of cooperative behavior in societies. Additionally, we discuss potential directions for future research, including investigations into how external influences impact the system, as well as the potential for connecting our model to theoretical concepts like the global attractor theorem. Alongside these discussions, we explore possibilities for relating our results to empirical data collected from observing the behavior of animals. Lastly, we outline plans for extending our model to incorporate additional aspects, such as the effects of memory on the agents' decisions, and consider the implications for models of collective behavior in general. Through this work, we aim to contribute to a deeper understanding of how the Motivation Dynamics framework can be utilized to study the emergence of cooperative behavior in complex systems.

The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Shwartz established a significant link between the ordered generating sequences and the standard Coxeter presentation. Our study extends this connection to the finite classical Coxeter group Bn by standardizing the ordered generating sequences, which allows us to identify exchange laws for Bn. Moreover, we establish a connection between the standard ordered generating sequences, Coxeter length, and the descent set of Bn. Our findings give the exact expression of Coxeter length and the number of elements of a given descent set in Bn. Furthermore, we develop a strong generating set for the wrester group of Bn, which gives the exact expression of its rank. Alongside, we discuss the properties of ordered generating sequences in the finite classical Coxeter group Dn. Our proof involves a novel interpretation of the standard Coxeter presentation of Bn, which is then an explicit expression of elements in Bn, followed by establishing the standard ordered generating sequences for the reflection subgroups of Bn. Our study offers both theoretical and practical applications of ordered generating sequences. It is an explicit, creative application of combinatorial techniques to non-abelian group theory. It gives new insights and properties of order generating sequences, which can be further used to investigate the wrester group, one of the most fundamental concepts in the field. Our study paves the way for exploring order generating sequences in other finite Coxeter groups and group theories. It also offers new methods to study the standard Coxeter presentation and the standard ordered generating sequences, which can be used to investigate the complex properties of non-abelian group theory. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. Furthermore, we established a framework to estimate the interaction strength between light and spin in these devices, showing that a large overlap between the optical transition and the spectral diffusion spectrum can result in significant spectral diffusion even at low laser powers. As a result, we suggest using the 220nm device layer of SOI wafers as a suitable material for quantum communication applications that require high scalability and integration levels. Additionally, we propose the use of T-type damage centers in bulk silicon as a suitable material for quantum systems that require long-term storage of quantum information, offeringcompromise between high density and long spin lifetimes. As the field continues to evolve, we believe that further research and development of this material will play a crucial role in the progression of quantum communication systems.

The high activity levels of M dwarfs present a significant challenge for discovering exoplanets, as their stellar activity masks the signals from these celestial bodies. This problem requires an effective method for filtering out the stellar activity from the data sets, especially when searching for habitable Earth-like planets. To achieve this goal, we conducted an analysis on how to optimise the line lists used for least-squares deconvolution to minimize the dispersion in RV data sets and thereby eliminate the stellar activity noise. Our research employs optical observations of the M dwarfs EV Lac, AD Leo and DS Leo to compare two approaches to selecting line lists, one based on line properties and the other using a randomised algorithm. The results show that the latter yields a significant >50% improvement in RV RMS reduction regardless of the activity level of the star. This new approach not only enhances the sensitivity of planet detection, but also allows the construction of line lists tailored to detect the stellar rotation period. Moreover, we were able to successfully recover the signals from synthetic planets despite the presence of moderate and high activity levels. This new approach is an important step towards developing a practical algorithm that can periodically monitor the stellar activity and filter out the noise in real-time data sets, thus accelerating the detection of exoplanets. This innovation will soon be integrated into the DIAMAN-TNG project. Until then, we will make our line lists available for other activities related to the study of M dwarfs. These line lists can be employed not only for the analysis of RV data sets and activity indices, but also for the determination of stellar parameters, detecting stellar spots and the analysis of photospheric abruptions during flares. This research provides a critical foundation for numerous upcoming surveys of low-mass stars, including the TESS Public Domain, and will ultimately facilitate a deeper comprehension of the properties of exoplanets. This understanding is essential for identifying suitable targets for future missions aimed at detecting biosignatures on habitable worlds. The main objective of this paper is to investigate multiple solution possibilities for a specific Kirchhoff type elliptic system of equations that are given by the system of equations where $m\left(\sum^k_{j=1}\|u_j\|^2\right)\Delta u_i=\frac{f_i(x,u_1,\ldots,u_k)}{|x|^\beta}+\varepsilon h_i(x)$ holds for $i=1,\ldots,k$, within the bounded domain $\Omega$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, where $x$ contains the origin with smooth boundary, and for a certain condition $\beta\in [0,2)$; here $m$ denotes a function that belongs to Kirchhoff type, $f_i$ behave like $e^{\beta s^2}$, and there is a function $h_i\in \left(\big(H^1_0(\Omega)\big)^*,\|\cdot\|_*\right)$. By making use of a singular Trudinger-Moser inequality for a small positive value $\varepsilon$ and variational methods, we are able to establish sufficient conditions for a multiplicity of the system's solutions given the given conditions. Additionally, we are able to demonstrate the existence of a function that reaches the level which the Trudinger-Moser inequality reaches, and this is achieved without the use of least energy ground state solutions. This is a key finding for the multiple solution theory. Furthermore, we are able to show that for a certain condition, there will be at least $k$ distinct solutions, provided that $f_i$ behave like $e^{\beta s^2}$. This is a result that is achieved by making use of a concentration variational principle, together with an estimate of the degree of solutions that concentrate in one point. This research is accompanied by several auxiliary results, including an analysis of an associated Kirchhoff type elliptic equation when $i=k=1$. This research is a continuation of the research as presented in Li et al. (2019).

We examine the concentration behavior of functionals of random vectors whose entries reside in the discrete cube. These vectors must adhere to either the stochastic covering property (SCP) or the strong Rayleigh property (SRP). Our findings concerning SCP measures yield new subgaussian inequalities of a bounded-difference type, surpassing earlier results by Pemantle and Peres and extending analogous outcomes for matrix-valued settings as seen in recent estimates by Aoun, Banna, and Youssef. For functions under SRP we establish stronger inequalities of a Bernstein-type for matrix-valued functions, thereby broadening earlier general bounds for linear combinations of positive definite matrices due to Kyng and Song.

Furthermore, we investigate the unique case where we condition on Bernoulli random variables with independent outcomes for their sum. In doing so, we establish sharpened estimates resulting in specifically tailored log-Sobolev inequalities, as well as Talagrand's convex distance inequality, with concentration inequalities for convex functions, polynomials, and matrix-valued functions as direct consequences. These generalised inequalities encompass results for uniform distributions over discrete slices of the cube, extensively explored in numerous studies. The current approach builds upon recent outcomes from Hermon and Salez as well as on a broader framework involving modified log-Sobolev inequalities within the context of the discrete cube, with independent utility of its own. 

Ultimately, conditionally on any given nonnegative definite matrix following SRP, we demonstrate that strong concentration inequalities of a Bernstein-type will hold for matrix-valued functions, with no need for independence among the random variables generating the matrix, thereby achieving independence from the underlying matrix structure. This outcome could be viewed as an indirect consequence of established general bounds by Kyng and Song for linear combinations of positive definite matrices, with a particular note that the current result surpasses those outcomes. The current approach also allows for sharper inequalities of a bounded-difference type for functions under SCP, with no need for independence among the random variables, thereby again achieving independence from the underlying structure. 

All concentration inequalities derived within this study will also hold in an averaged sense when conditioning on any given nonnegative definite matrix, with no additional condition required. Furthermore, we establish that the log-Sobolev inequality, with no need for independence among the random variables, will hold for the full distribution upon averaging over any given nonnegative definite matrix, with no need for independence among the random variables, with no additional condition required. This outcome could be viewed as an indirect consequence of established modified log-Sobolev inequalities

This study explores the double longitudinal-spin asymmetry in semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering where hadron pairs' transverse momentum is not considered. Specifically, we investigate the cause of the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in hadron production, accounting for the connection between the helicity distribution $g_1$ and the twist-3 dihadron fragmentation function. Using a spectator model, we calculate the interference term between $s$-wave and $p$-wave and estimate this asymmetry at various experiments, including COMPASS, JLab 12 GeV, and the future EIC. Our analysis suggests that the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in SIDIS can serve as a key test for the dihadron fragmentation function. Additionally, we demonstrate that the bond-boast asymmetry, defined by the ratio of the dihadron fragmentation functions, can be accurately determined through the use of a twist-3 fragmentation function alone, thereby providing a fundamental understanding of dihadron production in deep inelastic scattering. Furthermore, we estimate the dihadron distribution in the rest frame of the hadron system, anticipating notable variations in asymmetries at different hadron types, and propose extracting the dihadron fragmentation function at the EIC via an SIDIS analysis at small $x_z$, which would substantially enhance our knowledge of the twist-3 dihadron fragmentation function. Ultimately, this research positions the EIC as the ideal facility for a comprehensive investigation of the dihadron fragmentation function, unlocking the full potential of semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering as a tool for studying hadron structure in the context of quantum chromodynamics.

Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class. Following this discovery, Springer was able to develop a rigorous proof that the number of conjugacy classes in Sp_n(K) is equal to the product of the number of monic irreducible polynomials of degree d over K, multiplied by the number of pairs (e1, e2) where e1 and e2 are non-negative integers summing to 2, and further multiplied by the number of forms of three variables in the relevant equivalence class, but only considering classes that are self-dual. Notably, this finding offers a direct link between the conjugacy classes within the symplectic group and the polynomial values that the group can undertake, specifically focusing on the set of absolutely split conjugacy classes, thereby establishing a novel formula to calculate the number of such conjugacy classes. A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. A Markov Decision Process model is introduced, which accounts for the level of incompatibility as a key factor, making it a more complex problem to solve, but with suitable conditions, it is possible to establish control limit policies that can be easily applied. Our study uses numerical examples to demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves under different levels of incompatibility, and highlights the significance of taking incompatibility into consideration in decision-making, especially when desensitization treatments are available. Furthermore, it is shown that inferior policies can perform well in certain situations, where the costs of rejection and treatment are high, but it is possible to establish better policies when the costs are lower, but still significant, without relying on costly simulation feedback. Finally, it is shown that the optimal policy can provide a high quality of life for patients, even when incompatible kidneys are accepted, with a quality of life score above 0.8, indicating a relatively healthy life for patients. However, it is also shown that if the score is allowed to decline to 0.7, then the optimal policy would accept kidneys that could lead to a high risk of rejection, but it is not considered medically acceptable. Finally, it is suggested that individualized policies should be developed for each patient, taking into account their specific needs and circumstances, rather than adopting a one-size-fits-all approach. Keywords: kidney transplant, incompatibility, Markov Decision Process, control limits, quality of life.

This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. To address these challenges, we propose alternative approaches that integrate the learning of word embeddings and the selection of training data, enabling the effective extraction of sets of words exhibiting similar behavioral patterns from financial corpora. Our methods are designed to be flexible, allowing them to be applied to any corpus with identifiable word groups, such as genders or species in biological corpora. We provide both the mathematical framework and empirical evidence to support our claims, offering feasible solutions for the development of more accurate and versatile NLP models. We have made our code and data available for reproduction of results. We have also introduced our suite of tools for NLP applications known as "Embedding-verse" on our GitHub repository. We invite the community to collaborate with us and contribute to this initiative. We have shared our findings with the NLP community and have contributed our techniques to several leading NLP benchmarks, including the MultiNLI and CoLA tasks. We have employed our methods for the detection of allusions in financial news reports and the classification of financial rumors on micro-blogging platforms. This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries. To further improve accuracy, we've implemented Taylor--Hood nodal discontinuous pressure space for immersible boundary methods and presented melting boundary tests. Furthermore, we've demonstrated the feasibility of this approach for parallelization and explored its potential as a framework for modeling real-world applications involving fluid phase changes. This includes challenging situations charactized by moving and re-entering interfaces, where traditional methods struggle to perform reliably. In addition, we've highlighted key advantages of our method over other approaches, such as the ability to maintain accurate solutions in the presence of re-entering interfaces and the efficiency of Cartesian grids in handling complex boundaries. This research provides a strong foundation for the use of level-set methods on Cartesian grids in modeling fluid phase changes and related problems. It also paves the way for exploring more sophisticated applications, such as processes involving multiple phase changes and moving boundaries, and investigating new algorithms to enhance its parallelization capabilities. Current versions of the Lambek Calculus used in computational linguistics are expanded upon using unary modalities to govern structural rules affecting sentence order and phrasing. This incorporation of controlled structural operations yields derivational ambiguities missed by the original Lambek Calculus and its simplification in pregroups. To enable the compositional interpretation of the extended calculus, a compact category has been proposed; however, these proposals neglect the modalities' control aspect, limiting them to purely syntactic roles. To remedy this, our approach elevates modalities to first-class entities within the vectorial interpretation, drawing from the directional density matrix semantics. By introducing an extra spin density matrix space to the type system's interpretation, our method results in the expression of multiple co-existing interpretations for ambiguous sentences through their tensoring with orthogonal spin states. This method offers a unified framework for handling both lexical and derivational ambiguity within a sentence's interpretation. A lexicon based on this concept has been implemented and made publicly available under the name of MultiCoNLL. This implementation facilitates the interaction between the extended Lambek Calculus's semantic interpretation and the PCGR parser for Catalan. Moreover, our method predicts the expressional capabilities of categorical compositional semantics, allowing us to achieve notable performance in ranking interpreted sentences according to their likelihood in actual discourse. This indicates that the spin-based interpretation of the extended Lambek Calculus is a promising approach to addressing ambiguity issues within the categorical compositional semantics framework. Despite its potential, our proposed method is still in its nascent stages and requires further development to thoroughly address the challenges posed by ambiguity in natural language processing. The underlying theoretical density matrix semantics also has applications in quantum computer science, making this method a pioneering effort in the intersection of category theory, natural language processing, and quantum computer science. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. This research paves the way for the exploration of more intricate rationalizable solutions in multiagent learning. It is worthy to note that the developed algorithms are explicit, straightforward, and readily applicable across various multiagent learning contexts. Moreover, the results are expressed in terms of the number of actions rather than the number of states, providing a more manageable expression suitable for games characterized by a vast state space but a relatively small action space. The paper's findings introduce novel bounds that define the size of CCE and CE, providing a measure that is both rationalizable and minimizes (swap-)regret, thus addressing an unresolved problem mentioned in the 2020 paper. An analysis of a stochastic Susceptible to Infective to Recovered model is conducted, where the model is based on an Erdős-Rényi random graph that changes dynamically as susceptible individuals connected to infected neighbours form new connections or sever existing ones. As the model is scaled to accommodate large populations, researchers obtained mathematical proofs of key properties of the model, particularly its early stages and the phase where the epidemic spreads rapidly. They also found that under certain conditions, there are sharp thresholds where the model suddenly switches between two completely different behaviours. It has been proven that these transitions are more dramatic if the model is changed to only form new connections to uninfected individuals, where the model suddenly switches from no infections to complete spread. Researchers were also able to show that by increasing the rate at which connections are changed, the model can spread infections more quickly. Finally, they compared the model based on redundant connections to existing research on similar topics.

Initially, we establish the incompatibility of such solitons when the potential vector field is directly aligned with the Reeb vector field. Then, assuming the potential vector field is perpendicular to the Reeb vector field, we demonstrate that on non-Kenmotsu almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds with the Reeb vector field being an eigen vector of the Ricci operator, a steady Cotton soliton emerges, characterizing a manifold that is locally identical in geometry to the warped product space $\mathbb{H}^2(-4) \times \mathbb{R}$. Furthermore, this soliton is classified as non-degenerate, and its position depends on a scalar value related to the potential vector field. Additionally, we find that this soliton's configuration vector field can be expressed as a linear combination of the potential vector field and a specific gradient vector field associated with a function connected to the normal vector field of the Reeb surface. To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-of-the-art policy optimization methods. Additionally, it serves as a comprehensive toolkit for the development of exact diagonalization codes, carefully designed for high performance, ease of use, and customization. libcommute boasts an intuitive syntax for commonly applied abstractions and algorithms, and its extensive documentation and comprehensive unit tests guarantee its stability. Establishing the electronic and superconducting gap structure of iron-based superconductors requires in-depth microscopic understanding. However, even with extensively studied samples like (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$, there has been significant controversy over these structures. Our team resolves this by employing high-resolution ARPES on (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ utilizing both He lamps and laser sources, our results reveal the combined effects of band back-bending and band folding resulting in a flat band at the center of the Brillouin zone. Moreover, our data directly demonstrates the band folding in both superconducting and normal states around the zone center, allowing for correct assignment of the hole-like bands. Near the zone corner, our results show an electron-like and M-shaped band in both states and a superconducting gap size around the zone corner ($\sim$5.5 meV), contradicting previous findings. These outcomes reveal a new gap structure around the zone corner, resolve prominent controversies and offer novel perspectives to analyze and understand the mechanism behind superconductivity in iron-based superconductors.

Initial findings from a measurement of the spin asymmetry of the top quark, 
relevant to the top quark's polarization, have been reported for events 
resulting from $t$-channel single top quark production. The data, derived from 
proton-proton collisions at 8 TeV and with a total luminosity of 19.7 fb^-1, 
included events characterized by an isolated muon. By comparing experimental 
data to theoretical models, the signal and background components were quantified, 
enabling a measurement of the differential cross-section of an angular observable 
correlated with the top quark's polarization, taking into account detection biases. 
The results revealed a spin asymmetry value of 0.26, with a 95% confidence interval, 
which does not differ significantly from the standard model's predicted value of 0.44. 
This analysis's capabilities to address potential disconnections between the data and 
the standard model are showcased through several scenarios of new physics interactions. 
The research contributes to a deeper understanding of the standard model by limiting 
possible deviations from its predictions, with the results providing a spin asymmetry 
constraint for the first time ever. As a result, constraints on new physics interactions 
are formulated based on the observed values, which are found to be in line with expectations 
from the standard model, with no evidence of deviations up to a new energy scale of 26 
TeV, a result that holds true for various new physics scenarios. Nonetheless, this research 
facilitates a more precise determination of the top quark's polarization, which can be 
achieved in future experiments with enhanced luminosity and energy levels. This study's 
results will also contribute to a more accurate interpretation of new physics scenarios 
involving the top quark, such as extensions to the standard model with additional 
Z' or W' bosons, which can be further developed with more precise data. This research 
lays the groundwork for a more detailed analysis of the top quark, involving its 
polarization, which can be investigated through various angular observables in top 
quark production processes, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of the top 
quark's properties. This finding is anticipated to contribute meaningfully to the 
development of theories addressing new physics beyond the standard model. This is

We have conducted an in-depth examination of the correlated metallic state of LaNiO$_3$ using $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR within LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices of varying bilayer thickness. Our spin-lattice relaxation studies in a 6.55 T magnetic field yielded distinct components, characterized by different temperature dependences in their recovery times, with one being temperature-linear and the other exhibiting more intricate temperature variation. These results demonstrate that the slow-recovering component is resistant to changes in LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness, while the fast-recovering component is significantly affected, displaying an opposing temperature dependence in thinner samples. This complex phenomenon is explored to identify its underlying cause. Additionally, we obtained the spin-spin interaction and shift spectra, providing further insight into the microscopic structure and dynamics of LaNiO$_3$ within the superlattices. Our findings demonstrate that LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices possess the unique ability to host a persistent correlated metallic state regardless of layer thickness, offering a valuable property for further investigating the extrinsic effects on LaNiO$_3$. Our work also establishes the utility of $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR in probing LaNiO$_3$ and related materials, enabling the direct investigation of the spin-lattice relaxation and providing a wealth of additional information about a material's microstructure and dynamics. 

Our study has extended our understanding of LaNiO$_3$ in several ways. First, we have his initially reported data which showed that the spin-lattice relaxation rate in LaNiO$_3$ is abnormally high, exceeding the expectations of the Lindhard model by a factor of five. This abnormal relaxation rate is characterized by a linear temperature term in $T/\Theta_{\mathrm{EW}}$, with $\Theta_{\mathrm{EW}}$ being the Einstein temperature, and is resistant to changes in LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness. Secondly, we have uncovered opposing temperature dependencies in the LaNiO$_3$ layer with varying thickness, with the faster-recovering component exhibiting a more intricate temperature variation in thinner samples. The complexity of these results indicates that both intrinsic and extrinsic factors are influencing the spin-lattice relaxation process, and as such, our work lays the groundwork for a more in-depth examination of LaNiO$_3$ and related materials using $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR
