Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has surged exponentially with more than 10,000 online datasets now available and formatted according to Linked Data standards, enabling seamless machine readability and interconnectivity.  While such datasets provide numerous opportunities, numerous applications remain hindered due to data of poor quality, significantly affecting tasks such as data integration, search, and interlinking.  Existing quality assessment techniques for Linked Data, although limited, suffer from decreased effectiveness with rising data sizes and become unmanageable for single-machine operations.  To address these challenges, our proposed DistQualityAssessment is an open-source, cluster-enabled implementation designed for comprehensive quality evaluation of large-scale RDF datasets, leveraging the processing capabilities of Apache Spark to distribute quality metrics computation.  This innovative, distributed in-memory approach allows for flexible metric extension via a provided quality assessment pattern and, through seamless integration with the SANSA framework, has been successfully applied in at least three external use cases, showcasing its superiority over existing methodologies.  Our proposed framework, along with the associated datasets and a detailed tutorial, is now available for public access on GitHub, along with the related paper that has been accepted for publication at the Extended Demos and Industry Tracks of the 18th International Conference on Semantic Systems.  This demonstration and corresponding paper have been co-authored by S. Kihoro, A. Cruz-Lansac, A. Jialin Zhang, T. Dolenz, A. N. Shmueli, A. Frisch, A. E. Serrano, and H. Sumerow. When working with data generated by random processes, an appropriate model is often employed for subsequent statistical analysis, but the standard method of maximum likelihood estimation is vulnerable to model imperfections and data contamination. As alternative methods without assumptions about a specific model typically lose efficiency, this paper introduces a robust procedure for estimating parameters in discrete data sets based on a well-known distance measure. Specifically, this method defines and evaluates minimum density power divergence estimators for independent increments and Markov processes, proving its consistency and providing distributional results in the context of dependent stochastic processes, ultimately showing the method's advantages in comparison to traditional maximum likelihood estimation for common processes like Poisson processes, Brownian motion with a drift and autoregressive models. The paper also includes simulations illustrating the minimum density power divergence estimator's performance in relation to maximum likelihood estimation for AR models, and real-world applications to non-parametric density estimation for cancer incidence data and regression analysis of wind speed data. The associated benefits speak in favor of adopting minimum density power divergence estimators as a reliable alternative to maximum likelihood estimation for process data.  The R software package 'MDPD' is also available for implementing these estimators and associated methods.  The package includes minimum density power divergence estimators as well as their non-parametric counterparts for density estimation, a sample path generator for stochastic processes, and various utility functions for data visualization and other tasks.  The package can be obtained from the GitHub site https://github.com/ahmasht/MDPD or installed directly using the command install.packages('MDPD') from the R environment.  Full documentation of the package, including installation instructions and usage examples, can be found in the package's user guide available at https://ahmasht.github.io/MDPD/ or within the package after installation.  The guide is also published as a separate document titled 'MDPD Package Guide'.  The guide is regularly updated to reflect changes made to the package. As IoT systems shift towards Edge computing and less reliable infrastructure closer to users, the complex environments of IoT pose significant challenges for software developers when testing their applications. Although various testing tools are available for IoT, several issues persist, such as the absence of advanced features for logical dependencies, fault injection, and multi-platform testing. By utilizing Kubernetes and virtual testbeds, Frisbee speeds up the testing process by streamlining the setup of distributed virtual environments and enabling complex 'what-if' scenario simulations. The creation of realistic traffic scenarios through automation is the primary focus.
Currently used approaches insert virtual characters into the environment using predefined rules but struggle to capture the intricate nature of actual traffic conditions, ultimately resulting in a gap between artificially generated scenes and real ones. As a consequence, these simulation tools lack the required level of accuracy necessary to train self-driving vehicles. To mitigate this limitation, we propose SceneGen, a traffic scenario model that utilizes neural networks to bypass reliance on predefined rules. SceneGen is particularly adept at inserting a variety of virtual characters into the environment and accurately modeling their sizes, positions, and speeds. Through extensive testing on two large datasets, we demonstrate SceneGen's capacity to accurately mimic the distributions seen in real traffic environments. Furthermore, when combined with sensor simulation, SceneGen is shown to be an effective means of training perception models capable of performing well in real-world scenarios. Ultimately, our approach allows for the development of more accurate simulation tools capable of efficiently tracing the evolution of traffic scenarios over time. These datasets, containing over 300k characters and spanning various real traffic conditions in multiple locations, are designed to serve as a foundation for future advancements in traffic simulation. On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel periodic measures that are linked to index-2 normal subgroups within its group representation. These measures exhibit unique properties, such as being periodic and anti-periodic, and can be associated with the group's Coxeter anatomy. We establish the exact formulas for their frequencies and demonstrate that the anti-periodic measures sum to 1. Furthermore, we prove that the periodic measures correspond to non-trivial projections of the half-space measures of the Ising model on a Cayley tree onto its group representation. This finding parallels a similar result showing that the free fermion measure corresponds to the non-trivial projection of the half-space measure of the Potts model on a Cayley tree onto its group representation. Additionally, we explore connections to the group's end structure and determine the measures of measures-related types. Lastly, we discuss how these results can be extended to include the Potts model.

We have derived flexible criteria that can not only verify ergodicity across most known sequence combinations, but also enable resolution for some outstanding issues. Notably, our reasoning employs a novel ergodic variant of a technique initially explored by Peluse and Prendiville in establishing quantitative versions of the finitary Szemer\'edi theorem's application. Additionally, our findings establish a key connection between ergodicity and the occurrence of patterns within sets that exhibit quasi-arithmetic properties. This relationship demonstrates the efficacy of using ergodic tools to tackle problems focused on sequence-based scenarios. We have also established the convergence of square roots or other similar operations across ergodic systems, providing new insights that may be useful in addressing the converse of Bergelson's conjecture. Furthermore, our work identifies new diophantine applications for controlling the values of polynomials across subsets with quasi-arithmetic properties, especially when these subsets are defined using highly regular sequences. We have simultaneously developed a broader theory that enables the description of ergodicity dynamics within individual sequence contexts, allowing us to determine the rate of convergence or divergence depending on specific recurrence properties. We have also demonstrated the significance of this dynamics in understanding both local and global pattern occurrence within manageable sets and, interestingly, this understanding can be applied to obtain upper limits for the values of polynomials across certain subsets, even when these subsets exhibit minimal structures. We have concurrently established the effectiveness of our approach in providing a direct proof of the highly anticipated Conjecture C of Furstenberg, which asserts that for any polynomial $P$ and any system of integer sequences, the convergence across ergodic systems can be described as jointly ergodic or nonergodic, which implies that there exists an ergodic system that exhibits the behavior of convergence or divergence. We developed three-dimensional hydrodynamic models of superbubble formation to
study the early stages of superbubble growth from young coeval massive star
clusters located within low-metallicity ($0.02Z_{\odot}$) molecular clouds.
Specifically, we explored how pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae
affect superbubble dynamics and dust grain formation. Our goals were to
understand dust grain growth within clumps orbiting the superbubble, as well as
dust survival from supernovae in a highly distorted and expanding supershell.
The model accounted for cluster self-gravity and star cluster potential, while
considering cooling effects and dust influences, using a sophisticated cluster
synthesis model. Similar to previous research, clumpy media cause superbubbles
to become irregularly shaped and driven mostly by expanding hot gas through low
density pathways. Our findings show that in large ($\sim 10^7M_{\odot}$) molecular
clouds hosting large ($\sim 5.6\times 10^5M_{\odot}$) superclusters, dust grain
growth contributes $4.8\times 10^{-5}M_{\odot}yr^{-1}$ to dust accumulation
over 2.5 million years. However, pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae
increase dust supplies up to $\sim 1200M_{\odot} (M_{SC}/5.6\times 10^5M_{\odot})$, 
with $M_{SC}$ denoting the stellar mass of the supercluster. Consequently, dust
production by both grain growth and supernovae could lead to considerable dust
accumulation within low-metallicity molecular clouds, a process compatible with
galactic dust formation patterns during early cosmic reionization phases.

Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances, or far-field detection, is a crucial capability for autonomous vehicles operating at highway speeds. They need to be able to spot obstacles from afar in order to allow enough time for the vehicle to stop. Unfortunately, the majority of existing evaluation benchmarks, like nuScenes, don't emphasize this challenge because they only assess performance within a certain range. There are a couple of key reasons for this - firstly, annotating distant objects can be difficult because lidar sensors typically only return a limited number of data points at such great distances, with almost 50% of objects more than 50m away from the sensor containing zero data points. Secondly, the commonly used metrics for evaluating three-dimensional detection tasks apply the same tolerance thresholds to near and far objects, which isn't aligned with either human vision or the disparities seen in stereo images. As a result, the task of far-field three-dimensional detection has not been given the attention it deserves. For instance, it has long been believed that high-resolution RGB sensors are key to detecting distant objects, but a more in-depth analysis shows that lidar-based approaches outperform RGB counterparts on the existing leaderboards. To better assess this challenge, we created a new evaluation protocol and a far-field validation dataset based on the well-annotated scenes from the nuScenes dataset. We compared a variety of three-dimensional detection methods with this protocol and the results verify the widely-held assumption that high-resolution RGB does enhance detection in the far-field. We've also proposed an innovative fusion approach for detecting distant objects, which combines the capabilities of RGB and lidar sensors using non-maximum suppression, yielding significant improvements over state-of-the-art 3D detectors in far-field scenarios. Chemical reactions can be comprehensively understood through a primary analytical tool called the potential energy surface (PES) which maps the relationships between molecular nuclei and their energy levels. Nevertheless, this tool becomes impractically challenging to utilize because identifying a substantial number of ground states across the vast dimensions of PES requires an unreasonably large number of preparations. A recent study suggests utilizing a quantum machine learning algorithm as a more feasible approach. This model utilizes quantum data consisting of different nuclear coordinate-based ground state wavefunctions to prepare the desired states on the PES at will. A classical neural network transforms nuclear molecule coordinates into quantum variational circuit parameters and the fidelity loss function trains it to achieve optimal performance. Notably, this study found that, regardless of the complexity of molecules being studied such as hydrogen chains, water and beryllium hydride, just a small number of samples were enough to achieve high overlap rates with ground states in practice. A theoretical aspect also proves a limitation to these protocols suggesting it would be against the laws of physics if such efficient protocol could apply to regions where the ground state significantly drops in energy as in avoided crossings due to limitations imposed by Grover's lower bound. Also the amount of data that could efficiently be processed by the classical neural network is determined with respect to quantum data requirements from a quantum angle. Overall this study suggests that applications involving quantum chemistry are promising candidates to showcase the capabilities of quantum machine learning in action.

Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. The liver's featureless surface and varied image modality noises also pose significant challenges. We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset includes realistic biomechanical simulations of randomly generated organ models undergoing deformation. This allows it to efficiently apply to novel patient organs without retraining, also enabling robust performance against noisy intraoperative surface inputs during testing. The trained network provides an optimal displacement field to map preoperative volume to the intraoperative surface, demonstrated by multiple experiments showing its applicability and efficiency with real-world data. In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. We present a proposal to utilize a Random Neural Network as a versatile classifying model that combines the efficiency of spiking neural networks with the high classification accuracy achieved by traditional neural networks, showcasing this concept's effectiveness across real-world classification datasets. A major advantage of this approach lies in its simplicity, as the model's parameters can be learned through conventional stochastic gradient descent methods, making it an attractive alternative for resource-constrained applications. Moreover, this hybrid approach offers potential applications in continuous signal processing domains, such as audio signal classification. Experimental results using publicly available datasets demonstrate the efficacy of this proposal, and its scalability is validated using a leading cloud computing platform. Furthermore, we highlight the hybrid approach's versatility by adapting it to different spiking neural network simulators. A resource-efficient, neuromorphic system that combines the hybrid classifer with another random neural network-based feature extractor achieved exceptional performance in the MNIST dataset, surpassing prior achievements in low-latency, energy-efficient handwritten digit recognition. This ground-breaking work paves the way for the development of efficient, real-world systems that combine the strengths of spiking and artificial neural networks. Such hybrid approaches have the potential to address complex classification challenges in domains with continuous inputs, and they may also contribute to a deeper understanding of biological neural systems by identifying functional equivalents in neural networks that solve real-world problems. A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. We can disregard bipartite cubic graphs, as they automatically satisfy the E2F condition, thus our focus shifts to non-bipartite cubic graphs. A non-bipartite cubic graph with the PMH-property will satisfy the E2F condition, even though it is not a necessary condition. Our work involves introducing the papillon graph, an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs parameterized by two values. We then determine the parameters under which the papillon graph exhibits the PMH-property or E2F condition, as well as proving no two distinct papillon graphs have identical structure. This implies that the papillon graph can be used as a potential example for a cubic graph with the E2F condition, which cannot be obtained through composition methods presented in the 2012 paper by Szajewski and Wastlight. Our research also introduces new methods for identifying papillon graphs with the PMH-property or E2F condition, as well as determining all such graphs with a specific type of planar subgraph containing no triangles. This leads to a conclusion that all papillon graphs with the PMH-property have a specific structure, which can be expressed by two positive real values being less than 2. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using standard, reliable technologies, Timeloops features a simple and efficient design comprising less than 500 lines of code. Our research showcases the capabilities of Timeloops by implementing system call learning for individual services and a couple of benchmark applications employing Python Flask, Apache Thrift, and Memcached, among other technologies. Furthermore, we show that Timeloops' performance, despite generating a more limited system call filter, is comparable to that of an unsecured system. We also examine the security implications of using Timeloops and present various approaches to system call learning, including one that minimizes user data collection. Finally, we highlight potential future research directions for Timeloops and other system call learning systems. We have made Timeloops available online for anyone to use and adapt. We intend to evolve Timeloops into a full-fledged system call learning framework that can be applied to various operating systems beyond Linux. We also believe its open-source code will inspire other researchers to contribute to its development and encourage discussion on its limitations and potential extensions. Within an extension of the Standard Model featuring a $B-L$ symmetry, we introduce a pseudo-Goldstone boson dark matter framework where the imaginary component of a complex $B-L$ Higgs field constitutes the dark matter present in the universe. The universe's dark matter abundance is dictated by the Standard Model Higgs boson-mediated process, yet its interaction with nucleons via the exchange of Higgs bosons is heavily suppressed due to its pseudo-Goldstone nature. As a result, the proposed model avoids restrictions imposed by direct dark matter detection experiments. Furthermore, we pinpoint model parameter regions that replicate the observed dark matter density in accordance with the Large Hadron Collider constraints and the findings of Fermi-LAT and MAGIC in their dark matter search endeavors. Moreover, we explore the capability of future direct detection experiments to uncover or rule out these model parameter regions. Additionally, we examine the potential of the Large Hadron Collider to produce and study dark matter in the form of leptonic final states, including the collection of certain mono-lepton search signals that could emerge as a result of this process. The dynamics of soccer games mean even small moments can greatly impact the outcome, making players, coaches, and scouts intensely curious about how to act effectively in pivotal situations. In such moments, teams may lose possession of the ball or score, leading to a desire for an optimal course of action. To address this need, we propose a novel way to describe the game's state and a batch reinforcement learning method to train a strategic policy network. By analyzing the contextual aspects of situations, the network can provide the best action to increase the team's chances of scoring, drawing on real soccer data from InStat. In a large-scale experiment with 104 European soccer matches, we found our optimized strategy consistently outperformed the standard policy, and it even mimicked the behavior observed in real games. Notably, we observed situations where actions like committing a foul or kicking the ball out of bounds might be preferable to shooting, showcasing the importance of nuanced decision-making. The model's performance is impressive, but it's crucial to acknowledge its limitations, such as the reliance on real data for training and the potential risks of exploiting bugs in the soccer engine used to simulate the game. Despite these constraints, our research demonstrates the value of reinforcement learning in identifying optimal strategies in complex, multi-agent scenarios like soccer, and it lays the groundwork for additional innovations, like the integration of external data. Ultimately, this work has the potential to contribute to the development of more sophisticated soccer game agents and provide valuable insights into the game itself. The code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/hjdw/rl-strategic-soccer, and the data used can be found on OSF at https://osf.io/7cw5p/. The paper this code is based on has been accepted for publication in the Journal of Machine Learning Research. The paper can be found on the JMLR website at https://jmlr.org/submissions/vol15/huang13a.html. The current version of the paper is also available on ArXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.16235. The data used in this research is from InStat, a leading sports data analytics platform, and it comprises detailed records of 104 European soccer matches, covering nearly 10,000 situations. The key features of the data include the probabilities of scoring or losing possession of the ball in various circumstances, offering a comprehensive understanding of soccer games. The data is described in detail in the paper, and it serves as the foundation for the reinforcement learning approach developed

High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. Formulations for WRI and ESI are developed within a Lagrangian-based mathematical framework, and both can be viewed as weighted versions of the classical FWI. Conjugate gradient methods are also explored to solve the normal equation for an efficient solution, and both time and frequency domain formulations of the wave equation solver are feasible. Despite these developments, the challenge of the large storage requirement for time-domain wavefields through iterations remains, and two possible workaround strategies for reducing this demand are proposed, including extracting sparse frequency-domain wavefields or utilizing time-domain data rather than wavefields. Ultimately, both WRI and ESI are evaluated through synthetic and real-world examples, and the outcome shows that WRI outperforms ESI due to its ability to match observed data with a more accurate representation of wavefield components, rather than sources. Moreover, both WRI and ESI outperform classical FWI, and the latter also fails to match observed data with generated data at the same frequency, whereas WRI succeeds in doing so. Additionally, time-domain wavefields can be reduced to 5-10 frequency-domain wavefields per gram, and this reduction does not significantly impact the inversion result. Ultimately, both WRI and ESI can lead to improved seismic imaging, and time-domain wavefield storage requirements can be substantially reduced without compromising the quality of the image. Orfeo, an open-source Full Waveform Inversion framework that is freely available on GitHub, has been used to conduct these experiments. Orfeo can be acquired through https://github.com/CGPP-UANL/Orfeo or by sending an email to orfeocgpp@gmail.com. Orfeo includes the new wavefield reconstruction and extended source waveform inversion algorithms, as well as the reduction of time-domain wavefield dimensions to its frequency-domain equivalent, and the code used for the experiments reported in this paper is also attached as an appendix to this paper. We've developed an all-optical technique for producing optical nonreciprocity on a microchip, achieved through the process of quantum squeezing a specific mode in coupled resonator systems. A key factor in this method involves applying classical coherent light in a one-way fashion to parametrically pump a nonlinear resonator. This selective pumping induces a chiral interaction between photons within the resonators, allowing us to build optical diodes and quasi-circulators. Notably, we've demonstrated the functionality of these nonreciprocal devices even with weak input, using a combination of squeezed-vacuum fields and classical pump light. We observed isolation ratios greater than 40 dB in optical diodes, as well as a high fidelity rate for quasi-circulators. We also found that our method allows for low-loss optical communication. Furthermore, we've demonstrated the ability to control the flow of light through our system using a relatively weak control light, effectively enabling the development of nonreciprocal optical transistors. These advancements hold significant potential for developing a wide range of optical communication systems, including quantum networks.

We have presented the results from the AstroSat analysis of the high-mass X-ray binary X-ray pulsar IGR J19294+1816 during its Type-I outburst in October 2019. Timing and spectral data from the decline phase of the outburst revealed the spin period to be 12.485 seconds, with significant spectral features. A Quasi Periodic Oscillation was observed at a frequency of 0.032 Hz and an RMS amplitude of 18%. Our joint spectral analysis detected Cyclotron Resonant Scattering and an Iron emission line at 42.7 keV and 6.4 keV respectively, further highlighting the complex nature of this intermediate spin pulsar's behavior during its 2019 outburst. Comparison with historical data suggests that IGR J19294+1816 exhibits significant variability in its spectral characteristics, making it important to continually monitor this recurring outburst phenomenon. Continued observation of this intermediate spin pulsar from AstroSat will provide valuable insights into its behavior. To analyze the interplay of species competition and dispersal, an asymmetrical noisy voter model was developed for a regular lattice structure. The model allows one species to colonize nearest-neighbor sites, while another species can settle at any distance but is less successful in doing so. The model includes external noise, which can lead to random species swaps in the lattice. The combination of these dynamics results in various species competition outcomes, including the exclusion of one species, distinct population coexistence, or bistable coexistence dependent on the starting population ratio. The model shows that an abrupt transition occurs as immigration intensity surpasses a critical point, causing the irreversible decline of the species with shorter dispersal range due to a cusp catastrophe leading to half loop dynamics. The model also identifies that the disorder brought by the asymmetry and noise leads to a marked increase in the species' coexistence region compared to fair mixtures, which, however, eventually succumb to total dominance by the fair mixtures in a first-pass dynamic scenario. The influence of the two species' dispersal mechanisms and the two types of noise on the competition outcome is examined through the construction of phase diagrams in the parameter planes of asymmetry and noise strength. The model further predicts that the extinction of the species with shorter dispersal range can be prevented through the increase of two types of variables: the intensity of long-distance colonization and the intensity of external noise, which results from a cusp catastrophe analysis and is confirmed by Monte Carlo simulations. The model provides a framework for understanding the complex interplay of species competition and dispersal in regular lattice structures through the combination of analytical and numerical methods. The analysis of the model highlights the role of irregular dispersal as a key mechanism for the coexistence of competing species with different dispersal ranges. The model suggests that the coexistence of these species is highly sensitive to the changes of dispersal patterns and subject to abrupt transitions caused by alterations in dispersal parameters, which is a prerequisite for the model's applications in natural systems. The model's findings on the catastrophic effects of large-scale dispersal and the stabilizing effect of noise also have implications for our understanding of the competition between species with different dispersal ranges. The model's predictions are relevant to various natural systems characterized by regular lattice structures, such as animal colonies on rocks or tumors in living tissues, and can be extended to more complex network structures. The model's analysis of the competitive interaction between two species with different dispersal ranges provides a theoretical framework that can be expanded to include additional species with distinct dispersal patterns.

Ancient sundials served as primary timekeepers before the invention of mechanical clocks, with the classical Islamic civilization utilizing the Sun's daily movement to determine prayer times, often relying on sundials for this purpose. This knowledge eventually spread to Indonesia through Islamic cultural influences. Indonesian sundials developed as a reflection of local advancements in astronomy, technology, art, and architecture, with historical examples warranting detailed documentation and study, though often overlooked in existing literature. To collect necessary spatial and temporal information on these sundials, a citizen science initiative could be implemented, addressing research inquiries while promoting science education among the general public. This concept has been proposed as a framework, referred to as the Suryakala-Nusantara program, to explore sundials through citizen science methods. This work introduces the theoretical foundation and proposed approaches for data collection, incorporating historical documentation and online resources, with a planned evaluation of the program's effectiveness through a pilot study. The pilot study will be tested on sundials located within the Malang City area in East Java, Indonesia. The proposed approach includes conducting a meta-analysis of previous research, assessing the program's theoretical foundation, and outlining the pilot study's methodology. The pilot study aims to evaluate the program's citizen science aspects, with plans to present the implemented approach and share the acquired data as a starting point for further research and potential continuation of the Suryakala-Nusantara program. This work is scheduled to be conducted over a period of 18 months. The proposed approach is anticipated to yield research outcomes, provide training for citizen science participants, and offer a starting point for the program's potential continuation. The pilot study is expected to yield novel findings, incorporating new knowledge acquired through the proposed approach. The duration of this study is set at 18 months, with the expected outcome to be presented at an international conference in the form of a peer-reviewed paper. The study aims to lay the groundwork for the Suryakala-Nusantara program, but its success is dependent on the outcome of the pilot study within the Malang City area in East Java, Indonesia. This integrated network is critical in addressing future energy and spectrum shortages. However, these D2D transmissions and wireless link losses could significantly impede the data transfer rate. In response to this challenge, we propose introducing an intelligent reflecting surface. We then develop an optimization problem to maximize the data transfer rate while ensuring that power is generated and D2D communication speeds are met. This optimization problem requires significant computational resources, but we develop an algorithm that addresses this challenge with reduced computational demands. Finally, simulations confirm the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm. Notably, when the number of D2D communications and wireless link losses are mitigated with a moderate number of SISs, the data transfer rate can approach optimal performance. Additionally, when the number of D2D communications and wireless link losses are severe, the algorithm can still provide near-optimal performance with a larger number of SISs. Moreover, it is demonstrated that a central hub can transfer data to those in need and supply power to those who require it in real-time. Lastly, it is shown that the algorithm has reduced computational demands compared to traditional methods. In the future, this hybrid network has the potential to solve complex optimization problems and address pressing challenges associated with data, power generation, and spectrum usage. The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate 
given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Through numerical analysis, 
we investigate the potential for a phase plate to attain down to 1 Angstrom 
resolution on an uncorrected TEM. By examining various design features 
(fill-factor, pixel pattern, symmetry), we identify how they influence the electron 
probe size and current density. Our proposed designs exhibit probe sizes ($d_{50}$) 
as low as 0.66 Angstrom, indicating that a programmable phase plate with 
electrostatic elements can successfully rectify spherical aberration well beyond the 
1 Angstrom threshold. Furthermore, our study reveals that design simplicity 
considerations can help balance performance and complexity. Specifically, a simple 
design with a fill-factor of 50% and randomly distributed pixels yielded a $d_{50}$
of 0.67 Angstrom, underscoring the capacity of an uncorrected TEM to attain highly 
sensitive high-resolution imaging. Additionally, we explored the potential for 
charge-density-based designs and stacked phase plate configurations. Our findings 
also bring attention to the importance of experimentally validating proposed designs
through actual use of a programmable phase plate. Ultimately, this study provides 
theoretical evidence that a programmable phase plate with electrostatic elements 
can achieve superior results to previously reported data and offers practical 
considerations for its design. Human readers can find the full text of the paper at 
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S073945442300071X and the associated 
data at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ultramic.2023.070711 for re-use and validation.

The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on their ability to accurately encode user input to generate relevant and effective responses. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, the underlying representation of this encoding is often overlooked, which can hinder the model's performance in anticipating the next utterance. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics from human or automated sources is insufficient in gauging a model's understanding of dialogue language, prompting the proposal of a set of evaluation tasks to scrutinize the encoder representations used in these models. In experiments, our findings suggest that certain evaluation tasks prove more manageable for certain sophisticated architectures to grasp than others and, interestingly, that RNN-based architectures outperform Transformer models in these evaluation tasks despite underperforming them in standard text generation metrics. This suggests that encoder representations hold a different character and are influenced by factors such as context, sentence position, and word semantics, which can provide valuable insights into the understanding of dialogue language. Furthermore, our work highlights the advantages of integrating evaluation tasks during training, which leads to more effective performance in almost half of the evaluation tasks. This work aims to advance the assessment of dialogue models' understanding and offer techniques to enhance their performance in anticipation tasks. Alongside our code and data, we release a set of baseline models and evaluation tasks to facilitate the development of more sophisticated architectures that better comprehend dialogue language. This way, we are capable of crafting more precise models that are capable of anticipating the next utterance in a dialogue. This will not only improve the accuracy of text generation but also expand our knowledge of the fundamental nature of dialogue language itself. This knowledge can then be applied to different domains and settings, which requires a unique understanding that is distinct from the understanding of language in isolation. Ultimately, this work lays the groundwork for a systematic assessment of dialogue models' understanding, which is a crucial step towards the development of more effective data-driven dialogue models. This assessment should be complemented by a thorough analysis of evaluation tasks that highlights the challenges faced by different architectures in grasping the underlying character of dialogue language, as well as a comparison of models' performance in these evaluation tasks against their performance in standard text generation metrics. This comparison is necessary because the understanding of dialogue language is a different aspect of these models, and one that is distinct from their language understanding capabilities. This work also offers various techniques to enhance the effectiveness of these models in anticipation tasks, such as the incorporation of evaluation tasks during training, which leads to better performance in almost half of the evaluation tasks

Deep learning methods for LiDAR data analysis have revolutionized 3D place recognition in autonomous vehicles and robotics by improving local re-localization and loop-closure detection rates in complex environments. However, extracting robust, orientation-insensitive 3D descriptors from LiDAR data remains a persistent challenge. To tackle this, this research introduces a novel, range-based, deep learning network called AttDLNet that leverages an attention mechanism to selectively emphasize contextual and inter-feature connections. The proposed network is tested and validated on the KITTI dataset, with experimental results showing its enhanced performance and loop-closure capabilities when incorporating attention layers. The study indicates that adding this attention mechanism yields more efficient loop closures and outperforms existing LiDAR-based place recognition approaches. Moreover, results suggest that encoder layers with middle depths exhibit the best mean performance and exhibit robustness to orientation variations, with code publicly available for review and replication. Nonetheless, pure attention-based models lack sufficient context comprehension, prompting the inclusion of directional information via integration with RBF layers. The integrated model proves capable of full-loop closures on the KITTI dataset, with further research needed to attain similar levels of understanding in more complex urban settings. The work presented also raises thought-provoking questions about encoding orientation information and incorporating supplemental sensor data to enhance place recognition expertise. Streaming high-quality video, whether it's Video-On-Demand or live, demands transcoding to accommodate viewer devices. This requires significant computing power and, due to rising demand, streaming services now rely on cloud computing to ensure a seamless viewing experience. Cloud providers offer a range of Virtual Machines, each with varying capabilities and prices, which poses the challenge of optimizing cloud utilization for video transcoding. This study is the first to thoroughly assess how video transcoding performs across different cloud machines, which is essential for predicting processing times and developing effective scheduling methods. Based on this analysis and the cost variability of cloud machines, the research provides a model that helps evaluate the suitability of each cloud machine for different transcoding tasks. This model can provide resource provisioning with the best balance of performance and cost, thus enhancing the efficient use of cloud services for video streaming. The research provides a solution that can be integrated into existing video streaming services and can contribute to the development of cloud computing utilities. The methodology used in the research can be applied to other compute-intensive tasks, which could be valuable for cloud providers seeking to offer their services more efficiently. The study is pertinent to the growing trend of multimedia streaming services moving to cloud computing, as well as the increasing adoption of cloud utilities, which are often judged by their utility for processing multimedia content. We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material. The velocity of charge carriers can be extracted from the thermal capacity measurements, and we discuss the prospects of using this thermal capacity to diagnose the presence of zero-energy Dirac point zeros in graphene and other two-dimensional materials. Our study provides a thermal version of the Fermi liquid theory and offers a framework for investigating the thermal behavior of graphene and other Dirac materials at different temperatures.

Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. MaskedSpeech is a context-aware synthesis system addressing this limitation. By building upon a masking strategy, MaskedSpeech incorporates contextual acoustic features into each sentence, enabling a more detailed understanding of semantic relationships. Additionally, cross-sentence coarse-grained semantic features aid in the development of a natural prosody. Through augmenting masked acoustic features with contextual elements during training, MaskedSpeech outperformed baseline systems in expressiveness and naturalness. Our findings suggest that context-aware acoustic feature engineering plays a crucial role in speech synthesis. Moreover, by incorporating contextual semantic elements, fine-grained speech characteristics align with the context, resulting in an overall more natural speech pattern. Evaluations using both objective and subjective methods validate the effectiveness of MaskedSpeech. Compared to non-context-aware models, MaskedSpeech shows an enhancement of 13% in naturalness and 27% in expressiveness. Additionally, real user perceptions through crowd sourcing revealed a significant naturalness gain (11%) and the famous MAE reduced by half (50%). shifts in word meanings. We present an enhanced ensemble method that surpasses
earlier contextualized approaches and apply it to investigate the levels of
semantic change in English vocabulary over the course of 5 decades. Our
results show that contextualized methods may inaccurately predict significant
change in words with little to no actual semantic evolution, or whose

A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei
between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear
migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, we utilize extended, high-speed lightsheet and two-photon imaging
techniques in live zebrafish retinas during initial development to gain insights into the underlying mechanisms governing
the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM. Our high-resolution images permit us to accurately map the migration
patterns of multiple densely packed nuclei across the retina. By analyzing these migration tracks, we develop and test
a hypothesis that retinal IKNM is driven by a diffusive process fueled by the accumulation of new nuclei at the upper
retinal surface. Our results demonstrate how the tight packing of nuclei at the upper surface influences their movement
patterns, provide a reliable, quantifiable explanation for the uneven distribution of nuclei across the retina, and may
have implications for random cell fate selection within this system. Furthermore, we propose that retinal IKNM could
serve as a key example for studying the complex interplay between spatial organization, movement, and cell fate choice
within rapidly developing tissues. By integrating imaging, theoretical modeling, and biological experimentation, we hope
to shed light on the many universal principles governing this and other similar systems. The techniques and findings
presented here can be applied to further investigate the intricate behaviors of multiple densely packed migrating cell

This paper details a specialized apparatus built for use in Aberdeen Tunnel's laboratory in Hong Kong. The laboratory is uniquely situated to study spallation neutrons produced by cosmic-ray muons with 611 meters of water equivalent in depth. The apparatus consists of six layers of horizontal plastic-scintillator detectors that pinpoint the direction and location of incoming muons. Between these layers, a neutron sensor filled with 650 kilograms of liquid scintillator containing a gadolinium dopant significantly enhances detection efficiency of the produced spallation neutrons. Additionally, we discuss the performance characteristics of this apparatus. During testing, we recorded a neutron detection rate of around 50 per day, and measured the spectrum of super-neutrinofiltered neutrons. Furthermore, we collected data with both the super-neutrinofilter in place and removed, to develop a method for separating neutrons generated by muon interactions from those generated by other particles, including cosmic-ray protons. We also tested the apparatus's ability to correlate neutron production with specific components of incoming cosmic-ray muons, or with the direction of incoming muons. We plan to use this system to study the composition of cosmic-ray muons through the technique of ring-imaging, in conjunction with neutron detection, and to investigate the properties of void-space cosmic-ray spectra. Finally, we outline plans to upgrade the apparatus to enhance its capabilities.

Ground-based observations of planetary movements are crucial in validating the findings of space-based missions like Kepler and TESS. Although these missions show that planets are widespread, the success of these missions relies heavily on the use of transit photometry and ground-based radial velocity surveys to determine the physical properties of these celestial bodies. The TESS telescope is capable of identifying planets around bright nearby stars, which are ideal candidates for follow-up observations. We propose the TESS-Keck Survey to investigate various properties of these exoplanets. Utilizing 100 nights on the Keck/HIRES, the survey's primary objectives include analyzing how planetary compositions are linked to the characteristics of their host stars, understanding the diversity of planetary system architectures based on the planets' dynamical configurations, and pinpointing suitable targets for study with the JWST. We introduce a fully automated algorithm for selecting targets, which identified 103 planets across 86 planetary systems in the final TKS dataset. The stars hosting these planets are generally inactive, solar-like, and in the main sequence stage, with temperatures ranging from 4500 K to 6000 K and diverse metallicities. The TKS dataset comprises 71 small planets with radii smaller than four times that of Earth, as well as systems featuring multiple transiting candidates, short orbital periods, and planets situated near or within their host stars' habitable zones. The target selection strategy described can be adapted to facilitate the comparison of observational data with theoretical models of planetary population, and is openly available at https://github.com/ashleychontos/sort-a-survey, suitable for any survey that requires striking a balance between diverse scientific goals within a given telescope allocation. The methodology presented can be applied to any survey that requires comparing theoretical models of a population with observational data, and is freely available at https://github.com/ashleychontos/sort-a-survey. Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to evaluate the imaginary time path integral for these simulations. The imaginary time was incremented in small steps, with a quantum propagation time set to 0.01 units. A total of 1000 random walks were conducted to determine each expectation value. The quantum propagation time was chosen to balance the accuracy of results and the duration of computations. Higher driving strengths or larger masses required longer quantum propagation times to achieve the same accuracy, with theoretical limits applied to simulate quantum propagation times greater than 10,000. The stability of the ground state was confirmed by comparing simulations with driving frequencies greater than the natural resonance of the oscillator. The outcome of these calculations demonstrated that stable ground states could be achieved even when the driving frequency exceeded the oscillator's natural frequency. However, sharp resonances emerged at specific multiples of the oscillator's natural frequency, with significant amplitude fluctuations observed. Additionally, higher mass or stronger driving forces led to greater amplitude in the oscillations. The behavior of the oscillator under varying driving forces in both cases demonstrated the efficacy of this simulation approach. The quantum harmonic oscillator is a fundamental system that has been extensively studied to validate the principles of quantum mechanics and the development of quantum theory. The success of this simulation approach justifies its application to more complex systems, such as condensates composed of two or more oscillators. The availability of computational resources allows for precise simulation of quantum systems using a variety of methods, such as the lattice Metropolis algorithm, and enables the exploration of their physical behavior in greater detail. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be best measured through light curves as the phase shift accumulates over time in a quadratic manner. To study this effect in detail, researchers collected archived data and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro, before utilizing a light curve inversion method to match their shapes and rotation characteristics. By modeling the YORP effect and incorporating other relevant parameters into their analysis, scientists were able to detect the YORP acceleration in three asteroids and found that the YORP acceleration in all ten detected cases was positive, accelerating their rotations. Furthermore, incorporating solar precession into their algorithm revealed evidence of this phenomenon in the data obtained for Geographos, which may be a crucial feature that needs further explanation. Ultimately, a long-term monitoring plan for selected asteroids is proposed to continually study the YORP effect and its impact on their rotational states. Additionally, this study highlights the importance of combining YORP acceleration modeling with other processes when analyzing the orbital evolution of asteroids, and suggests that the YORP effect may be responsible for the formation of the binary asteroid system Tangra Da Qu and the extended orbit of its component, Tangra. The YORP effect is a critical factor in the evolution of small asteroids, and understanding its impact on their rotational states is essential for predicting future binary or broken asteroid formations. The most suitable targets for such studies should have visible light curves with measurable rotation and YORP parameters, and the largest group among them consists of binary asteroids with a total of 17 objects. We examined online discussions on Instagram in relation to politics from a network perspective, focusing on communities of co-commenters. Our analysis revealed salient co-interactions - instances of user engagement occurring more frequently than chance would suggest - to be crucial in driving online discussions and information dissemination. We based our study on 10 weeks of data surrounding key elections in Brazil and Italy, observing users who commented on posts from politicians and celebrities. We found communities centered on politics to be more active in discussions, with members producing longer comments containing more emojis, hashtags, and negative language compared to communities focusing on other topics. Additionally, we observed a diverse range of topics over time, with some topics receiving fleeting attention while others centered on fundamental issues continued to be actively discussed. Communities involved in politics displayed dynamic characteristics, with some users consistently contributing to discussions and retaining their status as top commenters. Furthermore, we identified users who frequently participated in discussions involving multiple communities and distinguished them as central figures within the Instagram political discussion network. These central users demonstrated a strong connection to the communities involved and often initiated discussions, further highlighting their importance. We also explored various features of comments, including language and content, to gain insight into online discussions and information dissemination. Ultimately, our study offers a comprehensive understanding of online discussions and information dissemination on Instagram through the analysis of commenters, communities, and the network that connects them. We are sharing our dataset publicly to facilitate further research into social media dynamics. It is essential to continue monitoring and analyzing the evolution of online discussions and communities to better grasp the underlying mechanics driving them. It is also necessary to explore methods for activating positive discussions that promote informed dialogue and counteract the spread of misinformation. It is possible to leverage the features of comments to develop automated detection tools capable of identifying central users, the duration of discussions, the language used, and the effectiveness of online discussions in relation to politics. It is also possible to employ machine learning techniques to analyze comments manually or through the extraction of hashtags, emojis, and other content features, ultimately offering a more detailed understanding of online discussions and information dissemination. Precise stellar characteristics are vital for both astrophysics and exoplanetary science, particularly when studying M-dwarfs. Researchers have developed numerous empirical relations that can utilize easily accessible observations to estimate stellar properties. However, these relations are often presented in a non-linear format, which is not suitable for Bayesian modeling. A novel Bayesian approach has been developed to consistently and simultaneously apply multiple empirical calibrations to accurately determine the mass, luminosity, size, and surface temperature of a typical M-dwarf. This new framework incorporates a mass-radius relation for M-dwarfs with a scatter of just 3.1% at fixed mass. The researchers also established the M-dwarf Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Sample (MUSS), and applied their method to obtain consistent stellar parameters for these low-mass stars. The MUSS targets are of interest primarily due to their potential to host exoplanets or serve as benchmarks for stellar activity across different wavelengths. Using the field MUSS stars, a mass range for low-mass stars in the solar neighborhood was defined through a process involving Gaussian Process regression. The resulting data show a distinct feature in the GP derivative, located at approximately 0.337 ± 0.013 to 0.026 M_(? ̇_odot) mass units, which indicates where the M-dwarf sample transitions from being fully convective in its interior to partly convective. The MUSS stars with surfaces completely convective in both the optical and near-infrared have lower Gosynski coefficients than their partly convective counterparts, showing a transition in the Muhanadi-Davenport relation. The new framework has been incorporated into the parametrization of the Muhanadi-Davenport relation, and has been successfully tested with mock data that mimics the observations of MUSS targets. The developed method is now an integral part of the exoplanet analysis software suite, CAPS. The researchers suggest their method provides the most accurate way to determine the properties of a typical M-dwarf, and is therefore the new standard for this class of stars. The MUSS targets, along with the method's implementation in CAPS, are now available in the form of three companion papers that include observational data, the MUSS target parameter catalog, and the CAPS modifications. The MUSS target parameter catalog contains consistent stellar parameters for 42 M-dwarf ultraviolet spectroscopic targets selected from the MUSS, and has been contributed to the third paper. Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to other infinite strings, including MSO-transducers, streaming transducers, and certain two-way transducers. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some functions in these models can still be undecidable by Turing machines with infinite input, despite being defined by finite-state machines. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine. 

For the type of functions in question, being computable is equivalent to having a specific property called continuity, effectively simplifying the original problem to deciding if a given function is continuous. To accomplish this, a more general rule is established to characterize continuous functions that preserve regular languages under a specific operation, and this is applied to demonstrate that continuity can be reliably determined for rational and regular functions. Furthermore, this decision-making approach is efficient and takes only $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$, a previously known but higher $\mathsf{PTime}$ requirement. 

Additionally, a more nuanced concept related to continuous functions is explored and related to its computable counterpart. This research provides a foundation for advancing the study of streaming transducers and other related topics.

Finally, an open question remains about the adequacy of MSO-transducers for capturing continuous functions with specific properties, particularly those defined by streaming transducers with read and write buffers. A corresponding conjecture suggests that such transducers can be equivalent to functions that have a different property called prefix-preserving continuity, a concept that is also of interest for further research. This relationship is to be determined for transducers with limited buffer capacity as well as those with unbounded buffers. This work also includes a new decision-making approach for determining if a rational or regular function is continuous, effectively allowing the computability of such functions to be decided in $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$. 

Furthermore, this research explores transducers with different types of memory, such as read-only or read-and-write buffers, and examines if they can be equivalent to functions that have specific properties, such as continuity or preservance of prefix-dependent behavior. This study provides a foundation for advancing the understanding of streaming and transducers and related topics. It also raises open questions about the relationship between transducers and functions with specific properties, particularly for transducers with limited or unbounded buffer capacity. This is particularly the case for determining if streaming transducers can be equivalent to functions that have properties such as prefix-preserving continuity

Multi-Layer Perceptrons are particularly effective at generating accurate
low-dimensional representations of data, such as images, shapes and light
fields. Despite advancements using periodic activations or positional
encodings, they have historically been tailored to process a single signal
and sacrificed some degree of generality. We introduce an innovative new
approach to representation learning that not only generalizes well to multiple
signals, but outperforms the competition in fidelity. We utilize a unique
two-part neural network design, where a synthesis network produces the output
given a point in space (like a pixel's position) and a modulation network uses a
given input's specific latent code to control the activation of this synthesis
network's periodic elements. We also develop an innovative local-function
approach to representation. It divides the input domain into uniform squares,
and each one has a unique encoded code. Then, at inference time, a highly
realistic representation of the given input is produced by either learning
or inferring the entire codebook. Our method produces general representations
for data, such as videos, shapes and images, outperforming previous methods.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by how entities are perceived as social agents. In this study, a stimulus set with independent factors of visual categorizability and agency perception in animals was used to test these hypotheses through both computational neural networks and behavioral experiments. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging, our findings showed that visual categorizability and agency perception separately explained independent components of the animacy spectrum in VTC. When combined, they fully captured the continuum, and our data indicated distinct posterior regions associated with each. The results of this study demonstrate the complex nature of the animacy spectrum in VTC, revealing multiple governing principles such as social agency that shape our understanding of this phenomenon. Furthermore, they suggest the existence of overlapping, highly localized posterior regions responsive to distinct aspects of the animacy spectrum. Ultimately, this research lays the groundwork for reevaluating previous studies on the animacy system and encourages the exploration of more sophisticated theoretical models. Through the incorporation of distributed neural representations and the examination of the animacy spectrum in relation to other dimensional systems, such as emotion and shape, our study provides a foundation for future research in this field. The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently intensified by a single high-transmission event, a super-spreader occurrence. This effect should be given considerable consideration in traditional epidemiological modeling, which requires reliable estimates of critical parameters such as $R_0$. We illustrate in this report that the effective $R_0$ value in scenarios featuring a super-spreader event is significantly elevated, with an order of magnitude equivalent to several hundred, which is indicative of a very brief period of rapid transmission during such events. A simulation involving a well-mixed space aligns with these findings and contributes valuable insights to modeling infectious transmission dynamics within enclosed environments. These environments diverge significantly from the parameters typically modeled in a standard SIR scenario. The proposed model also yields expressions that relate $R_0$ values to physical and operational variables of these closed spaces. The influence of a super-spreader event on public health is highly variable and ultimately depends on factors such as the epidemic's overall severity and how the virus transmitted through that single event continues to spread among community members. However, our analysis suggests that even a very small transmission of 0.1 persons per hour from a super-spreader in a scenario where community transmission is slow would still result in a substantially elevated $R_0$ value of approximately 33, which is significantly above the value that a effective intervention measures could tolerate for an extended period. The presented study provides novel insights into the complex transmission dynamics of contagious diseases, especially in closed spaces, and highlights the importance of giving due consideration to the effect of a super-spreader event in such scenarios. Additionally, it is crucial to conduct thorough investigations into the underlying causes of such events and their implications for the spread of the disease. The knowledge gained from this study can be applied to enhance the understanding of epidemiological modeling and contribute to the development of more effective strategies for containing the transmission of contagious diseases. We present a novel, direct method for calculating the decay width of hadrons
decaying to two photons, often requiring an indirect estimation via off-shell
form factors. The new method offers an uncomplicated way to study volume effects.
In an example calculation, we apply this approach to $\eta_c\rightarrow 2\gamma$.
Using lattice ensembles with three $N_f=2$ configurations at different lattice
spacings, we derive the final decay width $\Gamma_{\eta_c\gamma\gamma}=6.57(15)_{\textrm{stat}}(8)_{\textrm{syst}}$ keV,
considering systematics in the charm quark mass. This technique can be extended
to additional processes involving leptons and photons in final states. Through
correlation studies, we also extract the form factor at zero virtuality, enabling
us to compare our results to existing lattice QCD studies that have been determined
experimentally, providing a new perspective on $\eta_c\rightarrow 2\gamma$ observations. 
In the case of $\psi\rightarrow \ell^+\ell^-\gamma\gamma$, our method allows us
to determine the decay width into two photons and an $e^+e^-$ pair, yielding
$J/\psi$: $2.48(2)$ keV and $\psi':$ $0.53(5)$ eV, respectively. These
results are unambiguous and do not depend on the charm quark mass. We also
derive a quantitative expression for systematic uncertainties associated with
this method. To facilitate the calculation of direct decay widths to multiple
photons, we have developed a publicly accessible code called DIREC. Code available from a public repository mentioned in the paper.

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. This paper examines the relationship between integers that are y-friable (or y-smooth) and the Dickman function. By assuming the Riemann Hypothesis (RH), we had a previous estimate of the count of y-friable integers up to x in terms of the Dickman function but it was limited to integers y greater than or equal to $(\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$ due to previous work by Hildebrand and Saias. Without making any assumptions, we derive a more general formula that gives the count of y-friable integers for the larger range of $y \ge (1+\varepsilon)\log x$. This formula reveals a pattern that follows $x \rho(\log x/\log y)$ times correction factors. The correction factors consider the influences of zeta zeros and prime powers. By having this more general formula, we resolve two long-standing conjectures of Hildebrand and Pomerance. 

Hildebrand initially hypothesized that once $y$ is smaller than $(\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$, the count of y-friable integers would no longer follow the estimated $x \rho(\log x/\log y)$ pattern, which we confirm to be true.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its continued dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy. Our study offers data and findings that can assist researchers in the further investigation of online rumors as well as health-aware stakeholders in implementing more effective counter-measures. Furthermore, our methodology is versatile and adaptable to analyzing other types of information dysfunctions. A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. By focusing on the central areas, a comprehensive study has been conducted of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies located within the Fornax cluster using spectroscopic observations taken from the VLT/MUSE data collection from the Fornax3D survey. By distinguishing nebular emissions from stellar continuum and separating genuine planetary nebulae sources from false positives, a comprehensive database of 1350 distinct planetary nebulae was compiled across 21 galaxies. Each planetary nebula is associated with its specific location, luminosity of a particular spectral line, and velocity along the line of sight. By individually analyzing each galaxy, a reliable method for calculating the distances to galaxies has been applied using comprehensive planetary nebulae frequency distributions while also accounting for detection biases, and the resulting estimates of the distance to the Fornax cluster were calculated as 19.86 megaparsecs with an associated margin of error. Moreover, a significant dispersion was observed in the frequencies of planetary nebulae within individual galaxies, and a notable positive correlation was observed between these frequencies and the galaxies' overall mass, indicating that the detection of a significant number of planetary nebulae within a galaxy is a clear indicator of its massive nature. Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses. These analyses involve complex computations on significant datasets, necessitating high-performance data processing systems that can balance efficiency and simplicity. To address the limitations of existing data processing solutions, we present \emph{LifeStream}, a robust stream processing engine specifically designed to handle physiological data efficiently. LifeStream optimizes performance while providing intuitive temporal query language support, thus striking a balance between ease of programming and computational speed. Furthermore, LifeStream exhibits superior performance, outperforming other leading stream processing engines and hand-tuned numerical libraries by up to $7.5\times$ and $3.2\times$ respectively, on realistic datasets and workload simulations. Additionally, LifeStream's capability to execute queries efficiently, even with limited knowledge of performance-critical details, enables healthcare professionals to conduct repeated analyses with ease, facilitating faster diagnosis and treatment decisions. We highlight the significance of this work by demonstrating its practical applications in collaborating with clinicians to optimize cardiac surgery and streamline pregnancy monitoring. The engine's effectiveness is attributed to a novel hybrid approach combining simple in-memory computations with sophisticated output buffering strategies. We showcase the engine's core components, including its stream processing modules, temporal query execution mechanisms, and renowned optimization techniques, thus providing a comprehensive framework that is now available as an open-source platform. Experimental evaluations conducted with real-world datasets, obtained from top-tier hospitals, validate LifeStream's performance and practical viability. Furthermore, we introduce a user-friendly SQL-like language, named \emph{LifeQuery}, to facilitate easy query programming, reducing the need for expert programmers and lowering the barrier for healthcare professionals to conduct complex data analyses. We are now seeking collaborations with hospital research centers to leverage LifeStream's capabilities in various medical applications.
