The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. We further introduce a novel algorithm to adaptively adjust loss function weights in real-time, thereby enhancing model performance. Our experimental results across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate significant performance gains achievable through careful loss function design, leading us to propose the concept of Loss Function Tuning as a vital component of deep learning model development. Code is openly accessible on our GitHub repository https://github.com/hjdw2/LoCal. Our paper has been accepted for publication at IJCAI 2023.

A critical Sliding Mode control method is then utilized to drive the system from any initial state to a desired target state within a finite time, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed controller. One significant issue in Imitation Learning (IL) is that obtaining perfect optimal demonstrations from a teacher is a challenging task due to the complexities involved, especially in robotics. Providing quality feedback is further constrained by the need to supply demonstrations for multiple state actions at once. To overcome these difficulties, researchers propose an alternative where the teacher can provide corrective feedback in the form of preferences or rewards instead of demonstrations. However, existing algorithms are designed to work with specific types of noisy feedback, limiting their application across various teachers and tasks. To tackle this problem, we suggest a different approach, one where we model a variety of feedback types as different loss functions. Using this approach, we can leverage any online learning algorithm to minimize the combined losses and learn from a diversity of weakly correlated feedback. Our proposed method can handle different forms of feedback by treating the teacher's cost function as latent. By applying a general corrective feedback meta-algorithm that unifies prior work, we can achieve similar regret bounds regardless of the type of feedback. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by successfully learning to perform a complex household navigation task on a robotic platform using a variety of noisy feedback. Our findings show that our method can effectively learn from a different type of feedback that models the teacher's expectations and is significantly more efficient than alternative methods that can be designed specifically for the same task but with demonstration feedback. Additionally, we highlight the advantages of our approach by conducting human studies that show the diversity of feedback that can be obtained from a single teacher for the same task. Our method provides a viable solution for addressing the challenges of providing quality feedback in IL. Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Furthermore, it is proposed that the received signal be split into multiple branches with diverse delay periods, enabling efficient use of the available bandwidth and improved performance through post-processing. Current deep learning techniques used for removing rain from images have achieved notable success in processing artificially created rainy images.  Nonetheless, their effectiveness drastically drops when confronted with genuine rainy conditions, primarily because they often employ highly simplified models of rain which contrast with the complex real rain scenarios.  This study posits that rain simulation and elimination are mutually interconnected and hence need to be inextricably linked.  To accomplish this, a joint approach to learning real rain simulation and elimination within an integrated disentangled image transformation framework is proposed.  A proposed model involves bidirectional translation of disentangled images in two directions: the translation of real rain images into clear backgrounds, coupled with synthetic rain images.  Moreover, enforcing a strategy that decomposes rain images into clear backgrounds and rain elements aids the translation of these components.  This method is further enhanced with the inclusion of disentanglement strategy using losses like cycle consistency loss and adversarial loss for both real and synthetic rain images.  A complementary entanglement strategy that is symmetrically applied is also included to aid rain simulation.  Comprehensive experiments conducted on datasets of artificial and actual rainy conditions demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms other competing techniques. This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations. For specific $k_n$ values, particularly those of interest such as $k_n=\log n$ or $k_n=n^\alpha$ for $0<\alpha<1$, the established theorems provide specific asymptotic descriptions. Additionally, this work implies a central limit theorem for uniform random permutations, which are equivalent to conditioned random walks, and this central limit theorem is a key component in our proofs. The derived results and techniques also yield new insights and results in their own right. For instance, we obtain a new variance formula for the number of cycles of a random uniform permutation of size $n$ at $k$, and a variance formula for the number of avoiders in a random uniform permutation of size $n$ for specific patterns such as ascents or descents. Last but not least, this work also paves the way for future research by posing several open questions. One such open question is related to the asymptotic behavior of the smallest entry of $\pi_n$, especially when $\pi_n(1)/n$ is considered, and another open question regards the convergence rate of $\pi_n(i)/n$ for specific $i$ when the distribution is not uniform. Additionally, new results are also obtained for the sum or the maximum of the last $k_n$ parking locations, and this again depends on the specific structure of $k_n$. Lastly, a summary of known results for the asymptotic behavior of the first $k_n$ locations of a random uniform parking distribution of size $n$ is provided and organized by the specific distance metric

Broadbent and Lord introduced the concept of unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary can't produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. Our research expands upon this concept, focusing on several aspects:

  - Flexibility in Usage: We've identified a significant drawback in the previous unclonable encryption constructions by Broadbent and Lord, as they either only guarantee single-use security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. Our research presents two novel constructions for both public-key and private-key settings that maintain security even after repeated use and are founded on minimal assumptions.

  - Understanding Cloning Capacity: We've investigated the one-time secure construction proposed by Broadbent and Lord, specifically aiming to determine if achieving a nearly optimal $0.5^n$ success probability for cloning is attainable. Our findings generalize the construction based on various forms of monogamy of entanglement and present attacks against specific schemes with cloning probabilities reaching as high as $0.75^n$.

  - Applications to Copy Protection: We've discovered that strong forms of unclonable encryption can lead to enhanced security, specifically copy-protection for unlearnable functions. Our research paves the way for potential new constructions meeting these requirements, thereby expanding the realm of copy-protection methods. We've introduced two novel constructions for unclonable encryption and show its practical viability and potential connections to other fields, such as quantum cryptography and resource theory. We've also revealed multiple avenues for further research in this field.

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets. We observed improved generalisation performance, specifically on datasets requiring significant shifts, such as the voltage and luminosity changes in the MNIST dataset. We believe our findings offer a solid foundation for exploring the relationship between neural network sensitivity and performance in greater depth. We hope this work will contribute to the advancement of neural networks that are not only highly performing but also more robust in the face of data uncertainties. We also make available the code and data that underpin our study for the benefit of other researchers in this field.

Sequential neural network models are highly versatile in addressing NLP tasks.
Their sequential design leads to fundamental questions regarding their capacity
to learn complex language hierarchies and grammatical patterns naturally
occurring in human language.
As a case study for understanding the implicit comprehension of sentence
structure and the adoption of a complex yet systematic morphological system,
we explore agreement prediction in Basque, which demands a thorough analysis
of both.
Our analysis of the results of verb number prediction and suffix recovery in
two experiments indicates that sequential models perform below expected levels
on the Basque agreement prediction compared to similar models tested with
English data.
Our exploratory findings based on diagnostic tools indicate that neural
networks may leverage local strategies to compensate for their limited grasp
of hierarchical sentence structures.
As such, we introduce the Basque agreement prediction task as an ideal
benchmark for testing the language-learning abilities of neural network models. 
The code for our work can be found at: https://github.com/DonostiaBCG/basque-agreement-b0/tree/main/basque_agreement_prediction. 
The data used is based on the work by Lersch and Macdhonnghaile (2019) available at: https://github.com/hft/inferran. 
The code for our diagnostics can be found at: https://github.com/DonostiaBCG/basque-agreement-b0/tree/main/basque_agreement_diagnostic. 
The data, models, and protocol for our experiments are fully reproducible. 
The results of our work raise fundamental questions about the potential of neural
network models to learn complex sentence structures and imply that such models
may require additional mechanisms to fully comprehend the underlying grammar
and hierarchies of human language. 
As such, they have significant ramifications for the broader field of NLP. 
In particular, they suggest that neural network models should be subjected
to rigorous structural probes in conjunction with straightforward syntactic
analysis when operating in conjunction with morphological systems or when
attempting to interpret ambiguous sentence constructions. 
Ultimately, our study sets the stage for a thorough examination of the
implicit comprehension of sentence structure in neural network models across
all domains of human language. 
In addition to this, our results provide the Basque agreement prediction
task as a fully reproducible benchmark for testing the language-learning
abilities of neural network models. 
The code for our work can be found at: https://github.com/DonostiaBCG/basque-agreement

We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies. Furthermore, this code can be adapted to facilitate the search for vector leptoquarks in other processes, such as those involving the collision of protons at higher energies and involving the collision of electrons and protons. As a result, we provide recommendations for the parameters that could further enhance the effectiveness of these searches. A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based method, the study examines if modern computer systems that recognize connections within a text align with the principles of CT. The analysis indicates a correlation between the systems' ability to recognize connections and their ability to model the coherence of the text, but also reveals that these computer systems are not necessarily improved by considering the ideas underlying CT. Furthermore, the study finds that these computer systems already incorporate the coherence information required to recognize connections within the text, making CT's contribution limited. Additionally, the study discusses aspects that influence connections within the text but are not accounted for by CT, including the systems' knowledge and their tendency to favor more recent statements. By incorporating these elements, the study presents a revised version of CT and shows that it better captures the connections within the text compared to the original CT. The revised version of CT also demonstrates a clear distinction from the systems' ability to model the coherence of the text. The study's findings suggest that while CT provides valuable insights into connections within the text, it requires further development to fully capture the underlying mechanisms governing discourse coherence. The proposed revised version of CT can serve as a starting point for this development. By incorporating both conceptual and computational perspectives, the study aims to advance the understanding of the relationship between CT and the computer systems that analyze discourse coherence. The revised version of CT is available online for public use, providing a foundation for further research and encouraging discussions with other researchers who share this goal. The study's results can also be utilized in various applications related to the analysis of discourse coherence, such as enhancing the clarity of written texts and improving conversation evaluation metrics. The revised CT is offered as a starting point for these tasks and is compatible with other advanced computer systems that identify connections within a text. The study's results are robust across two datasets, describe a prominent mechanism governing connections within the text, and are clear enough to be interpreted by humans. The proposed revised CT is made publicly available to support conversations with other researchers and is ready for application in various scenarios related to discourse coherence analysis. This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately verifying that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems in alignment with the universal operator growth hypothesis. Moreover, our work showcases the value of leveraging Lie symmetry, which streamlines calculations and renders existing approaches like the Lanczos algorithm superfluous, instead allowing us to extract crucial insights through symmetry-based arguments. By distilling the underlying principles behind the operator growth phenomenon from this perspective, we are able to identify the underlying mechanisms driving it. Additionally, our work paves the way for the application of quantum information theory to systems of this type, which in turn may help inform the development of new algorithms for these systems.

Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings. Current works in constrained imitation learning have addressed various constraints but have left the issue of nonlinear hard constraints unresolved. To tackle this, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) which addresses multiple challenges in imitation learning, including nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP can learn from multiple demonstrations, adapt skills to various target points, avoid obstacles, and meet complex linear and nonlinear constraints. Our work also establishes connections to state-of-the-art motion planning methods, and we provide evaluations of our framework through joint trajectory planning for a 7-DoF robotic arm, demonstrating its effectiveness. The code for our research is available online at the specified link. Through our work, we aim to contribute to the development of learning hierarchical robot skills and to provide a foundation for future exploration in this area. This paper's findings have been accepted for publication in the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems.

In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. Although this calculation was constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations. In such scenarios, six-gluon amplitude functions can be expressed using impact factors, trajectories, CEVs for single-emission processes, and a residual component defined by conformally invariant cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may be used to create fault-tolerant quantum computations via topologically non-Abelian states. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with doping. Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling enhances s-wave superconductivity, overcoming Zeeman field-induced pair-breaking when present. Additionally, we demonstrate that Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance caused by the Zeeman field through mixing, thus restoring superconductivity. Furthermore, we established that Rashba coupling's favorable impact on superconductivity originates from a spin-flip driven enhancement of the likelihood of a pair of electrons traveling in reverse time-states. Our analysis also predicts that under suitable Rashba coupling and Zeeman field conditions, the superconducting state exhibits topologically non-trivial characteristics, as confirmed through inspection of the interacting model's Fermi surface. Courtesy of Rashba coupling, the superconducting state becomes topologically non-trivial even when the Zeeman field induces significant pairing correlations between opposing spins. By utilizing sound wave velocity and absorption measurements in very strong magnetic fields, we have found a previously unobserved state transition in the interlocked vortex lattice structure of the doped material La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$. The discovered phase shift, occurring at magnetic fields higher than 35 T and very low temperatures below the critical point without magnetic field, can be identified by measuring the stiffness of the interlocked vortex lattice, at a doping concentration of $x=p=0.17$. Our theoretical calculations using the Eilenberger theory for interlocked vortices demonstrate that this transition represents the expected rotation of the square lattice structure by 45 degrees predicted for materials that are $d$-wave superconductors near a point of high singularity. The high requirements for measuring this transition are due to the need for very strong magnetic fields that can override the material's normal magnetic properties, as well as the necessity for very low temperatures to do so, under conditions where the superconductivity remains unaffected in a specific area around the singularity point. The discovered transition provides a clear method for confirming the $d$-wave nature of superconductivity in materials that are structurally similar to La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$. Finally, by analyzing the shape of the transition by increasing the doping concentration, we have found that the critical point for the rotation of the square lattice structure by 45 degrees is around $x=p=0.05$, which is the doping concentration at which the highest singularity of the material's energy gap is located. The results of our study have significant implications for the study of interlocked vortices in superconducting materials that are $d$-wave superconductors, and have paved the way for a more in-depth investigation of the physics of interlocked vortices in La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$.

Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we predict how the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching change with mean and Gaussian curvatures, offering a detailed understanding of how surface curvature affects brush geometry and free energy calculations. This comprehensive knowledge can be utilized to simulate a broad range of brush geometries encountered in the assembly of block copolymer melts. In addition, this research has the potential to contribute to the development of various surface-sensitive techniques that utilize depth sensing and could benefit from brush geometry calculations. In particular, we propose the utilization of curved brush models in relation to the Elneview algorithm, a method that utilizes brush geometry to calculate optical properties. This study offers a crucial step towards developing accurate theoretical predictions for the geometric and thermodynamic properties of elongated polymer brushes on complex curved surfaces. It also paves the way for the simulation of brush geometry to enhance the Elneview algorithm's capabilities in calculating the optical properties of block copolymer films with elongated brushes. Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Furthermore, this method could be adapted to analyze images produced by other space telescopes and even narrow-field observations. While there are challenges to be addressed, this research offers an exciting potential for enhancing the sensitivity and accuracy of image analysis in astrophysics. Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We also examine issues of honesty and provide ways in which some of our solutions can be implemented fairly with incentives based on payment schemes such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves method. We propose and evaluate a new metric, the price of serial dictatorship, offering a quantitative indicator of the efficacy of combinatorial optimization solutions obtained via action sequences. We provide concrete examples and empirical evidence showing that our proposed action sequences result in acceptable social welfare in various applications, including image segmentation, multi-agent pathfinding, and general combinatorial optimization domains where simple 2-approximation algorithms are applicable. for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal less than 10 documented binary asteroids within this size range, with
orbital separations exceeding 10% of their primary components' Hill radius, it is 
essential to discover additional wide binary asteroids to clarify binary
stability constraints and enhance asteroid mass comprehension. Our analytical 
process for each image involved two approaches: firstly, by correlating the 
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF with its sidereal motion across 
the sky, and secondly, by creating a one-dimensional profile from collapsing the 
image along the asteroid's trajectory, and comparing it to that of nearby field 
stars. Any marked deviations from typical measurements of single asteroids 
were identified and flagged; among these flagged targets, the most notable were 
designated binary prospects awaiting confirmation through high-resolution 
imaging. From a total of 4575 reviewed images, our techniques identified 59 
potential binary asteroid prospects, with 13 confirmed through high-resolution 
imaging, and the remainder waiting for verification. Among these prospects, 
10 were discovered and added to the existing record of wide binary asteroids, 
while 3 were added to the list of wide separation targets awaiting confirmation 
or orbital data. By incorporating these discovered binaries, updated constraints 
for binary stability and asteroid mass are presented, showcasing how previously 
recorded binaries align with these new guidelines. Lastly, we outline the advantages

The South Atlantic rift basin formed as part of a large intraplate rift system separating Africa and South America during the Gondwana supercontinent's break-up in the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.  Analyzing crustal deformation in Central and West Africa enabled researchers to reconstruct the pre-break-up history of the conjugate West African-Brazilian margins.  Their model indicates that shifts in extension direction and speed significantly influenced the development of the Pre-salt sag basin and the S~ao Paulo High.  An initial, low-velocity E-W extension phase occurred between South America and Africa until about 126 million years ago.  Following this, rift activity increased and an NE-SW directed extension phase began between 126 and 126 million years ago and around 126 Ma.  In this 17 million-year period the conjugate Brazilian and West African margin Pre-salt basin widths were generated.  An intermediate phase of 126.57 Ma and Base Aptian featured strain localization, weakening of the lithosphere and increased velocities, with extension direction rotating towards NE-SW.  Breakup occurred around 113 Ma and then between South America and Africa.  It occurred again at 103 Ma, with this multi-velocity, multi-directional history having a strong effect on conjugate passive margins.  This is evident in structural styles, isostatic equilibrium, and stratigraphic patterns observed in 2-D and 3-D data.  This research offers a new perspective on the development of the South Atlantic rift basin, challenging previous models based on static palinspasts.  It also highlights the value of integrating geological and geophysical data, as well as numerical modeling, to explore the evolution of extended crust.  Finally, it suggests the importance of cross-African/conjugate margin research in understanding the development of rift and passive margins.  This type of research can offer new insights into the physics of extension, breakup and early oceanic basin evolution, as well as contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of the history of the Gondwana supercontinent.  It can also facilitate predictions about the distribution of non-rift related Pre-salt hydrocarbon systems in the South Atlantic basin. A proven strategy to enhance multiple tasks using limited labeled data is
unsupervised pre-training.  Despite being a viable approach, contrastive
learning poses challenges in forming relevant pairs for an unsupervised
segmentation task. To circumvent these challenges, our proposed framework
utilizes two primary components:  using unsupervised over-segmentation with
mutual information maximization and a pre-training task along with boundary-
preserving learning.  The experimental outcomes of applying our proposed
framework to two benchmark medical segmentation datasets demonstrate its
efficacy in improving segmentation accuracy with limited annotated images. 
Notably, our method successfully reduces the gap between annotated and unscaled
images, resulting in superior performance when applied to new unseen datasets. 
The code is available at:  https://github.com/zyang53/Unseg-misozoo. 
In particular, our method achieves outstanding results on ACDC (0.75 Dice score)
and Segercard (0.79 Dice score) validation sets, outperforming previous
state-of-the-art models by significant margins of 11% and 12% respectively. 
Furthermore, our method boasts the capability to segment 128x128 pixel images
with just 8k parameters, offering immense potential when applied to real-world
segmentation tasks. 
In addition, our method succeeds in identifying rare diseases by identifying
disease-specific features, thus showing immense potential when applied to very
small datasets. 
Ultimately, our method extends the capability of medical segmentation to
unsupervised scenarios, making it an extremely promising baseline for future
research.

and are accepting new task submissions at:  https://unseg.is.tue.mpg.de.

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. Additionally, we uncover that incorporating a Dopamine-like value estimation method amplifies the benefit, while we also identify challenges posed by the complex, multi-turn nature of these conversations. Our success paves the way for future exploration into how natural language dialogue can be fine-tuned to align with shared goals. This study deviates from this focus, shifting towards change discovery - identifying previously unknown word meanings emerging over time within a comprehensive corpus vocabulary. This distinction between change detection and discovery is a subject of ongoing debate, with implications for the field. Furthermore, our work presents an exclusive opportunity for cross-theoretical discussion and development within the area of semantic change research. By analyzing the Planck cosmic microwave background and the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey's large-scale structure, we discovered varying results due to limitations of current constraints, specifically volume effects that influence model parameter choices. Employing an unbiased statistical analysis technique called a profile likelihood to assess EDE parameters, we determined a confidence interval of $f_\mathrm{EDE} = 0.072\pm 0.036$ ($68\%$ C.L.), providing a clearer picture of EDE and its potential solution to the Hubble tension. Furthermore, we investigated the stress of existing assumptions on our findings and confirmed that EDE could account for as much as $0.1$ of the total energy density today. Additionally, we analyzed the case where an EDE model is scaled by a factor without altering its kinetic behavior, which could be supported within the $68\%$ C.L. and may resolve the Hubble tension to some degree. However, this scenario still falls short of fully addressing the tension. Nonetheless, our study maintains that EDE exists and deserves further investigation through additional data, particularly the information that will be obtained from spectroscopic measurements of massive galaxies and quasars in upcoming experiments such as the Square Kilometre Array. With such data, we anticipate that the discrepancy known as the Hubble tension will be clarified more clearly.

A detailed investigation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures drawn from Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra was discovered in a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios associated with the anomalous NG theorem. Notably, this algebraic structure can cause deviations from the conventional Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which could potentially be experimentally verified. A framework for effective potential formalism was developed to better understand the mechanisms driving the anomalous NG theorem. A study of a bosonic kaon condensation model incorporating a finite chemical potential served as an explicit example of Lorentz-symmetry breaking. A general discussion on the anomalous NG theorem has been presented through the lens of this model's Lagrangian approach. Moreover, this investigation uncovered both the criteria necessary for true NG boson generation and the mechanism for producing the masses of massive NG bosons. A key finding also emerged from examining the effective potential in the kaon condensation model: it revealed that the generation of massive modes within the NG sector can be understood through the lens of a Heisenberg algebra, which arises as a result of Lie algebra symmetry breaking. Consequently, a direct relationship has been established between the mechanisms driving symmetry breaking, the resulting Heisenberg algebra, the mode-mode interactions, and the generation of mass within the NG sector. Finally, some intriguing connections between the Riemann hypothesis and the anomalous NG theorem have been presented. Although much remains to be understood about these connections, they do underscore the importance of approaching the anomalous NG theorem from a variety of mathematical perspectives, including both Lie algebras and number theory. A summary of the proposed project is provided in the form of several open questions at the conclusion of this investigation. The related effective potential approaches to the mechanisms driving the anomalous NG theorem have the additional benefit of also clarifying the underlying physics governing the generation of mass within the NG sector. It is our hope that this study will not only shed new light on the anomalous NG theorem but may also contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex relationships that exist between Lie algebras, geometry, number theory, and the mechanisms driving symmetry breaking and mass generation within the NG sector. Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings. Ultimately, we observe that these improvements translate to real-world applications, yielding a 2% enhancement in semantic similarity and a 10% improvement in textual entailment. The code and data generated through this framework are now available at https://github.com/google-research/disco.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy. Finally, combining remote epitaxy with post-epitaxy etching of the substrate and surrounding material could provide a viable path to manufacturing high-quality Heusler compounds for spintronic devices.

A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unconditional and conditional GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data while significantly reducing the required annotation. Moreover, the technique proves particularly beneficial for GANs trained on datasets with limited annotation. This study seeks to create advanced mathematical methods and computational tools to model portfolio returns, establishing essential formulas and efficient algorithms using techniques from computational geometry and splines. By leveraging these methods, our approach can efficiently handle large portfolios and accurately compute moments of the probability function within seconds. We primarily focus on the long-only strategy and develop an adaptable method for this type of investment. By representing the stock market as a geometric space, our cumulative distribution function enables a score for each portfolio based on the percentage of its returns exceeding a certain threshold. We derived closed-form equations for the first four moments and an innovative algorithm for computing all other moments, demonstrating a direct connection between the cross-sectional returns and the moments of the distribution. All of our methods are highly versatile, covering scenarios including when asset returns are equal. We used our score-based approach to design new performance metrics and found the portfolios it produced less concentrated and less prone to high risks than those from the mean-variance model. Our method for computing moments is also highly valuable itself, providing insights into the characteristics of portfolios that have high moments. For example, we found that low returns in portfolios are often due to a single poorly performing asset, while high returns result from a combination of satisfactory stocks. To further aid investors, our method enables the creation of customized reports highlighting the key factors contributing to portfolio performance. Such reports can be particularly helpful in the asset management industry, enabling managers to measure the effectiveness of their strategies and pinpoint areas for improvement. We put our methods through rigorous testing on extensive datasets of random and real-world stocks, ensuring our algorithms can handle any portfolio size and cross-section of assets. We also explored various applications of our score-based approach, including the study of portfolio liquidity, risk, and performance trends over time. Furthermore, our method enables the analysis of custom portfolios and extends to modeling returns for sets of portfolios, enabling the investigation of how groups of portfolios perform in relation to each other. We constructed a standalone software program utilizing our score-based approach, which is available for public use and can be used in conjunction with popular financial software, such as Excel or MATLAB. We expect our methods and software to contribute significantly to the development of computational financial economics. Despite our focus on the long-only strategy, our methods and software can still be adapted for other investment scenarios with minor modifications. We also explore alternative score functions and show that our methods and software can be used to model returns for other financial instruments beyond stocks. We conclude by highlighting potential directions for further research, such as extending our methods to modeling returns for sets of portfolios

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates versatility, extensibility, and vast potential applications in the healthcare industry. The source code for FedHealth is freely accessible on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/cghs2018/FedHealth. The paper's findings have been publicly hosted on the following page: https://cghs2018.github.io/FedHealth/.

In large-scale organizations, recruiting involves interviewing a substantial number of applicants, a time-consuming and intricate process. To achieve efficiency, a well-planned approach to selection is crucial. This process comprises multiple, interconnected problems, each mirroring a well-known computational issue. While individual research has been extensively conducted, an integrated examination of these problems is uncommon. This paper addresses two critical aspects of application processing: creating review and interview panels and scheduling interviews. We developed a prototype system to automate interview planning for a real-world scenario. Compared to existing, manual methods, our approach yields a superior plan. To achieve this, we evaluated different algorithmic options and tailored them to solve panel creation and scheduling issues. We experimented with these solutions using real data, presenting our findings. This study may serve as a starting point for further development aimed at fully automating application processing processes. All implemented algorithms and test data are available for replication and extension at this link: https://github.com/AleksiZala/InterviewPlanning. This study tackles a complex control issue, where the costs of transitioning between states can change suddenly in time. Our main achievement is to derive multiple ways to characterize the optimal cost function, as well as to demonstrate the existence of policies that minimize costs under this dynamic framework. Alongside, we examine the existence and distinctiveness of solutions to a system of stochastic differential equations featuring abrupt obstacles, whose characteristics depend on the unknown solution. Finally, the paper also considers the case when the underlying system includes a random movement, resulting in the optimal payoff becoming a solution to a quasi-variational HJB PDE system with discontinuous barriers. This research is an extension of prior works on smooth costs in references [8, 17]. Unlike those studies, our environment entails regime changes that can occur simultaneously with optimal strategy transitions. This similarity to [11] exists in our specific setting where the filter's optimal policy can cause the regime to shift, a phenomenon also observed in the general case discussed later. The paper's first part addresses the existence of optimal control under different norm definitions. The second part explores the existence and uniqueness of solutions to the system of SDEs with abrupt obstacles, further extending the discussion to include the impact of filtration on regime changes in the third part. The paper's final section considers the quasi-variational HJB PDE system with discontinuous barriers in the presence of random diffusion. It deals with a scenario in which the same sequence from a specific set undergoes
different channel transmissions and yields distinct outputs at a decoder.
Assuming that the original transmitted sequence maintains a distance of d from a particular code
and includes at most r errors per channel, the sequence reconstruction task is
determining the least amount of transmission channels needed to obtain an accurate
replica of the original transmitted sequence.
It's also essential to note that this number must surpass the maximum possible
overlap between two spheres in a metric with a radius r, where these two spheres
have centers that are at least d units apart.
In this research paper, we examine the sequence reconstruction problem for permutations
under a specific distance metric known as the Hamming distance.

and determine the exact value of the maximum possible overlap between two spheres in
this metric with r = 4 and a distance of d = 5, or with a distance of d = 2r.

problem that was initially posed by Levenshtein.

Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional information-seeking datasets that typically consist of fact-based questions, the proposed QASPER dataset contains a diverse range of questions over 1,585 NLP research papers. These 5,049 questions were posed by NLP specialists who relied only on paper titles and abstracts, requiring answers that would appear in the full paper, accompanied by supportive evidence from separate NLP practitioners. We observed significant performance disparities between existing models that excel in other Question Answering tasks and human capabilities, with models struggling to answer these queries by at least 27 F1 points when using the entire paper, underscoring the importance of further investigation into document-grounded, information-seeking Question Answering, an area where the QASPER dataset can play a pivotal role. The code, data, and experiments are available at https://github/qasper.

We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a second-class particle placed at the origin, will asymptotically converge to a velocity whose probability distribution is uniform across the interval $[-1,1]$ as time tends to infinity. This conclusive finding addresses two unresolved conjectures from "The TASEP speed process" and enables us to develop the ASEP speed process. Additionally, we can directly apply this discovery to demonstrate that TASEP's speed process also converges to a probability distribution that is uniform across the interval $[-1,1]$. Moreover, we can use the comparison technique to show that the ASEP speed process can be lessened by multiplying the TASEP speed process by a factor of $\frac{1}{2}$. Lastly, we can use the COPE rule to establish a speed process for the partially asymmetric exclusion process.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control. Consequently, researchers, policymakers, and analysts must closely collaborate to develop, evaluate, and utilize models in this ongoing public health crisis. Ultimately, this collaboration is crucial not only for addressing the current pandemic but also for preparing strategies to deal with future outbreaks and the evolving challenges they will pose.

We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation from initial spinless atoms through two-body interactions equivalent to an effective three-body recombination. In our study, we also investigate the impact of light-based association and initial magnetization when a precise condition is met. Furthermore, we explored two scenarios: one in which the dark state condition is met imperfectly, either generally known as the adiabatic case, or not at all. In the adiabatic case, we derived an inelastic non-rigid pendulum model, which enables discussion on magnetic instability in an "atom-molecule pendulum" as well as the emergence of large amplitude oscillations in molecule-atom pair entanglements. In the non-adabatic case, we derived a complex quantum pendulum model that includes a spin-exchange driven molecule-atom pair oscillation between two potential wells and an associated rotation within those wells. Both models provide clear, qualitative insights into the complex quantum dynamics of atom-molecule systems in one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. In the case where the dark state condition is not met, we found evidence for the creation of molecule-atom correlations, referred to as an effective three-body effect, resulting from two-body interactions alone. Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless internal storage capacity. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired parts of the index, allowing us to precisely locate specific objects within a segment with minimal scope, resulting in the reduction of sequencing costs by up to 140x for the retrieval of smaller data objects. The advantages of this new architecture are demonstrated through the efficient storage of large, structured data sets, including a scientifically relevant example involving gene sequence data. The versatility of this DNA-storage design is showcased by its application to two very different data sets with fundamentally distinct data architectures. The functionality of this novel storage system has been realized through a working prototype, offering sequencing cost savings of up to 140x for object retrieval. The scope and capacity of each segment remains virtually unlimited, allowing for practically endless data storage within each 20-base PCR address space. The ultimate potential of this DNA-storage system is its ability to provide a robust, efficient, and versatile architecture for the permanent storage of program code and data. The versatile nature of this DNA-storage design is underscored by its successful adaptation to the rigorous requirements of a full-fledged programming environment, encompassing compilers, interpreters, utility programs, library routines, kernel code, and implementation of a multi-threaded programming model. The successful realization of this DNA-storage system has a significant bearing on the field of molecular computing, proving that a full-fledged programming environment can be executed from a DNA storage device, thereby establishing the feasibility of executing programs from DNA storage media in a practical context. The prototype of this DNA-storage system has a functional architecture comprising eight segments, addressed by distinct primer pairs, and has achieved successful demonstrations of data exchange between host computer and DNA storage device, execution of programs from DNA, and the retrieval of program code and data from DNA using PCR. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines. This includes the need for more realistic simulations and new experimental techniques to accurately study the properties and interactions of nodal lines in artificial materials. This review shall serve as a foundation for researchers to further explore the unique properties of artifical topological nodal lines. This is an open access article distributed according to the Creative Commons Attribution License.

Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, rigid pose, and geometric deformations from images. Moreover, this framework offers a way to learn the illuminant's spectral properties directly from raw images, without relying on the CMR factorization. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by recovering various scene properties, including coefficients for more complex illumination models and geometric parameters of rigid and deformable objects, and even recovering the spectral properties of the illuminant directly from a single image. All the code is openly available at https://github.com/lingidriver/SparseHarmonic-Differentiable-Rendering. Visual results can be found in the supplementary material. Our approach has the potential to become a standard tool for image-based rendering and is no longer a preliminary stage, given its high performance and accurate results. Nevertheless, there are still limitations to this approach, is it suitable for handling dense occluding surfaces or multiple light sources. Future work can be done by extending this approach to these scenarios. Additionally, this methodology could be useful in other areas such as enhancing digital content or reconstructing scenes from multiple images. However, this would require a more comprehensive approach that considers various sources of information. Lastly, while the illuminant can be directly learned from an image, the model is still highly regulated and a more flexible model is required that can handle a wide range of illuminants and scenes. Consequently, this approach has the potential to become a standard technique for image-based rendering, however, several challenges need to be addressed before it can be applied to a broader range of scenarios. Finally, we believe that this approach has the potential to be a foundation for other research, it could be interesting to explore other applications such as enhancing digital content, reconstructing scenes from multiple images, relaxing regulatory constraints, and developing more flexible illumination models

This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual electromechanical heart simulation. Findings reveal that the BDDC method offers highly efficient solutions for these intricate cardiac mechanics problems, even when the grid resolution is extremely fine. Nevertheless, the research also uncovers instances where the AMG method outperforms the BDDC algorithm, and identifies potential areas for enhancing the performance of the BDDC method. The research data has been utilized to develop an efficient solution strategy for solving cardiac mechanics problems, and the findings have significant implications for improving the speed at which heart simulations are conducted. The research advances the capabilities of its researchers to prepare complex cardiac mechanics problems for solution, and the efficiency of the BDDC method for these types of problems will contribute to the development of more effective solution strategies for other complex financial element applications. The project, undertaken by advanced graduate students, enables them to acquire a comprehensive understanding of how to effectively utilize high-performance computing resources, develop and assess the performance of sophisticated solution methods, and prepare complex financial element applications for solution. Recent studies have uncovered the prevalence of gradient masking in purportedly robust adversarial defenses. Consequently, defense strategies based on this concept are considered ineffective and can be readily bypassed. Notably, research into quantifying the occurrence and extent of gradient masking across different networks remains limited. This study addresses this gap by exploring the mensurability of gradient masking as a multi-dimensional rather than a binary phenomenon. In addition, we introduce novel metrics designed to evaluate the presence of gradient masking in diverse neural networks. These proposed metrics not only offer computational advantages but also facilitate comparative assessments between models without necessitating elaborate tailor-made attacks. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the efficacy of these metrics in gauging the prevalence of gradient masking across different network configurations. This, in turn, provides valuable insights into the inherent properties of neural networks in relation to adversarial robustness. This knowledge can be utilized to inform the development of next-generation neural networks that inherently incorporate mechanisms enhancing adversarial robustness, thereby obviating the need for complicated defense strategies. This concept is substantiated through numerical simulations, network architecture experiments, and comparative analyses of our proposed metrics in contexts involving multi-dimensional gradient masking. This research paves the way for a fresh perspective on the adversarial robustness paradigm, involving the exploration of methods that train neural networks with intrinsic resistance to adversarial attacks, eliminating the need for cumbersome defense strategies. This study provides a foundation for investigating other concepts of inherent robustness in neural networks. This experiment has significant implications for advancing the Adversarial Robustness (AdRoB) research field. Recently, proposed bianisotropic acoustic metagratings offer promising possibilities for passive acoustic wave manipulation, notably in flat acoustic lenses and ultra-high frequency ultrasound imaging. This concept, however, has not yet been implemented at the MHz frequencies common in ultrasound imaging due to difficulties in fabricating complex microstructures. Advances in two-photon polymerization now enable precise manufacture of sub-wavelength structures in this range. However, shrinking structures in size introduces another challenge, where increased thermoviscous effects lead to considerable energy losses, which need to be factored into the design. This work introduces three novel microacoustic metagrating designs capable of refracting normally incident waves by approximately 35 degrees at 2 MHz, utilizing shape optimization techniques and the linearized Navier-Stokes equations. Using two-photon polymerization, we fabricated and experimentally validated microscopic acoustic metamaterials, successfully redirecting incident waves and verifying that a 0.29 wavelength-thick microacoustic metagrating can efficiently allocate 90% of transmitted energy into the -1st diffraction order. This breakthrough paves the way for optimizing microacoustic structures for specific applications and fabricating complex acoustic lenses and sonwedges. Furthermore, it was observed that this model successfully recreates turbulent velocity patterns at Reynolds numbers that it was not originally trained on. Through the process of removing specific scales of turbulence (carried out by forcing turbulent flows with wave-like motions), it was revealed that this model's ability to recreate high-resolution velocity patterns is largely scale-transferrable. The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. This approach involves introducing an extra dimension to account for uncertainty and proposes an innovative energy-based objective function to unify both classification tasks and uncertainty modeling. Furthermore, theoretical analysis reveals that optimizing this function effectively captures the marginal data distribution in the uncertainty dimension. Our experiments demonstrate that Energy-based Open-World Softmax, this proposed method, outperforms current best practices in enhancing confidence calibration. The benefits of this approach are particularly evident when testing unknown classes, as predicted uncertainties can be leveraged to inform resource allocation and model improvement. Additionally, our work offers an actionable solution to the ongoing challenge of activating unused neural classifiers. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies. Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be paired with the Keck All-sky Precision Adaptive-optics system to optimize performance. By covering the wavelength range from 0.81 micrometers to 2.45 micrometers, Liger combines multiple observing modes, offering various spatial scales and fields of view. This processing system, called the Data Reduction System, will be responsible for delivering refined data to astronomers and uploading it to the Keck Observatory Archive. We have established a prototype of this data processing system and defined the communication interface with the relevant software systems at the observatory. In operation, the prototype will receive raw data from the instrument, refine it, and upload the results to the archive. We have successfully tested this prototype with actual data and are in the process of integrating it with the observatory's software systems. Once integrated, we plan to further develop the prototype in collaboration with the observatory, aiming to implement a production-ready Data Reduction System by the time Liger becomes available for astronomical observations in 2023. Subsequently, we will utilize this prototype to refine its output in real-time during feasibility tests scheduled for 2023 to 2024. Ultimately, this prototype will serve as the foundation for the data processing system on other future infrared instruments at the Keck Observatory. Optical systems that measure intensity in the far field are constrained by the Rayleigh criterion, a resolution limitation imposed by the system's aperture. Research has shown that using spatial mode demultiplexing (SPADE) allows for maximum collection of field information, thereby surpassing the Rayleigh criterion in certain cases. While previous SPADE approaches have relied on resolving the lateral splitting of a Gaussian wavefunction, our work investigates a novel scenario in which one of two photons from a bi-photon source, generated through spontaneous parametric down-conversion, undergoes a horizontal separation. Through coincidence measurements following the projection of both photons onto Hermite-Gauss modes, we demonstrate the ability to super-resolve this separation, a capability not attainable via standard SPADE techniques. Furthermore, our approach enhances the associated Fisher information by a factor of $\sqrt{K}$, where $K$ represents the Schmidt number that quantifies the entanglement between the two photons. Our findings indicate that SPADE of this type can provide a more efficient approach to achieving super-resolved imaging, likely utilizing fewer optical components. Moreover, our research offers a general framework applicable to a wide range of bi-photonic states and could lead to novel strategies for optimizing SPADE based on the characteristics of specific entangled photon sources. Ultimately, our work paves the way for the development of more efficient SPADE systems that can offer profound improvements in super-resolved optical imaging performance. Consequently, this technology has the potential to greatly enhance the fundamental limitation known as Fovea's curse, which poses a critical constraint in optical imaging, specifically in optical micro-imaging, optical atomic physics with optical tweezers, and optical communication based on entangled photons. This note provides an introduction to the interplay between Hodge-theoretic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties. It offers an early survey of developments in this area, covering key concepts and results from the 1960s to the 2010s. Specifically, it examines how both methods employ the fundamental properties of algebraic varieties, focusing particularly on the involvement of the Kodaira-Spencer approach, the period map, and the role of Hodge-theoretic invariants in this process. It also explores the interconnections between the Kodaira-Spencer equations, the compactification of moduli spaces, and the intersection properties of algebraic cycles. Moreover, it highlights the most notable results from this period, including the completion of the moduli space of algebraic curves, the construction of stable reduction for abelian varieties, and the proof of weak approximation and stable rationality for varieties of minimal model type. It also touches on later developments, citing works on Hodge-theoretic approaches to studying moduli and their connections to number theory and the arithmetic of algebraic varieties. It also mentions the role of mirror symmetry in this area, the application of Hodge-theoretic invariants to number-theoretic problems, and the potential for the field to contribute to the arithmetic of algebraic varieties. It also includes an overview of the methods and the core problems of the field, along with potential future directions for researchers. It is intended as a primer for researchers who are new to the field but have a background in algebraic and analytic geometry. It is based on earlier surveys by Iano-Yaseen, Ray, and Zhang but offers a more comprehensive and up-to-date review of the subject, along with new insights and perspectives. It is available as a book chapter in the volume 'Algebraic Geometry--Bowdoin 2019--Proceedings'. It is also available as a separate paper on the arXiv server. It is the first part of a larger project to create a comprehensive textbook on the subject. It is hoped that it will serve as a key reference for researchers in the field and will help to pave the way for a new generation of researchers who are looking to explore its many exciting possibilities and applications.
