We introduce a rigid cluster model to achieve a representation of the quantum group U_q(g) for Lie algebras of type ADE. This involves establishing a natural isomorphism from the quantum group U_q(g) to a subalgebra within the quotient of Weyl group invariants from the Fock-Goncharov quantum cluster algebra O_q(P_G ∘). Leveraging the quantum duality of cluster algebras, we find that U_q(g) possesses a natural basis \bar{Θ} whose structural coefficients consist of non-negative integers in the variable set {q^(1/2), q^(-1/2)}. Furthermore, the basis \bar{Θ} maintains an invariance property under the braid group action defined by Lusztig, Dynkin's automorphisms, and the star anti-involution. Consequently, the basis \bar{Θ} provides a significant improvement to existing constructions of quantum group bases, such as Lusztig's, Darboux's, and Capelli's, enabling the derivation of explicit formulas for the structural coefficients, and facilitating the extension of quantum group algebra U_q(g) to the realm of non-commutative partial derivatives for Lie algebras of type ADE. Lastly, our approach yields deeper insights into the quantum cluster algebra O_q(P_G ∘), revealing that it serves as the natural context for the quantum group U_q(g), and enabling the formulation of quantum group U_q(g) through its connection with the Dynkin diagram. Moreover, our results suggest the possibility of extending our approach to super quantum group U_q( rak{g}) and hyper quantum group U_q( rak{g}).

In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD, yielding an improvement of up to $10\%$ in test accuracy over various data distributions. DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds by up to $20$, compared to traditional DSGD, while also ensuring fairness across decentralized devices. Our research extends the application of DRO models in real-world scenarios with significant data sets, encompassing image recognition, language models, and recommender systems. DR-DSGD is readily available for public use on GitHub. https://github.com/hongdh/DR-DSGD. Our research paper is founded on the theoretical framework outlined in [1] and is complemented by an additional paper focusing on enhanced relaxation methods [2]. Like various simple scientific models, such as the Drosophila model, understanding the hard-disk model required significant effort. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. With almost 8,000 users and having paid out nearly 2 million dollars in withdrawals, Forsage's success serves as a prime example of the appeal of cryptocurrency-based pyramid schemes. To prevent recurrence of such schemes, we stress the importance of combining blockchain's transparency with user protection measures, including requiring two-factor authentication and limiting withdrawal capabilities. Additionally, we suggest that a notation method is introduced to represent the interactive scripts used in smart contract analysis. Lastly, our research introduces the concept of analyzing cryptocurrency-based pyramid schemes as a category of multi-level marketing businesses. With almost 2 billion dollars being lost annually to multi-level marketing scams in the United States alone, a comprehensive examination of these hidden transactions is more feasible now than ever before with the use of public blockchain data. As such, we propose ForPy, a framework for analyzing Forsage, as a potential case study for blockchains and a possible framework for analyzing other cryptocurrency-based pyramid schemes. By combining ForPy with ForForsage, our case study of Forsage, we believe this research offers a premier example of a pyramid scheme built into a blockchain, along with possible insights for blockchains and the overall framework for analyzing such schemes. This research is offered with the hope that it may spark further discussion and potential collaboration on the analysis of cryptocurrency-based pyramid schemes, particularly those built into blockchain smart contracts, as well as the potential use of ForPy for other such schemes. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to converged first-principle simulations to validate our TB models' accuracy. The results indicate that the dipole-based model yields a more precise description than the velocity-based model. We attribute this to the imperfect compensation of diamagnetic and paramagnetic currents in the velocity-based model. To rectify this shortcoming, we formulated a sum rule that explicitly addresses the compensation issue, allowing the correction of velocity-based models to match dipole-based models and guarantee gauge invariance. We further establish that this compensation issue arises from the use of incomplete basis sets in the finite tight-binding models. Consequently, we provide a second approach to correcting the velocity-based models, specifically aimed at mitigating this compensation error, which originates from the absence of certain tight-binding parameters associated with higher-energy states. The accuracy of both approaches has been validated through the simulation of electromagnetic responses. The methods presented in this study offer valuable insights into the development of reliable TB models for two-dimensional semiconductors and insulators, facilitating a thorough understanding of the fundamentals of light-matter interactions in these materials. The techniques described here have the potential to be extended to other solid-state materials and insulators. We study the behavior and evolution of Boolean networks with sparse connections that interact with themselves using Glauber dynamics, where the dynamics occurs simultaneously for all elements in the network. Equilibrium is evaluated by modifying and applying a method for systems that update in parallel. Similarly, dynamic behavior can be assessed using an advanced version of the method for systems that update at different times. Nonetheless, applying this technique to networks that interact with themselves is challenging because it causes the network to rely heavily on past events, making it difficult to model the network's behavior over extended periods of time. However, it has been proven possible to transform the network into an equivalent bipartite network with double the variables, allowing for analysis of systems that interact with themselves using traditional methods. This breakthrough enables a deeper examination of how systems behave during transitional and extended periods of time. Lastly, we investigate networks that interact with multiple components and are utilized in gene regulation systems by transforming these systems into equivalent bipartite networks that interact through pairs of elements. It is shown that these types of systems, where the flow of information is bidirectional, have the capacity to develop multiple equilibrium states, a key requirement for systems that manage life across various cell types. Moreover, we demonstrate that systems with permanent memory components are incapable of achieving equilibrium in a meaningful amount of time. Consequently, this research implies that secondary gene regulation is likely managed by systems that interact with themselves through external influences rather than internal processes. Finally, we propose that our findings can be experimentally validated through synthetic biology experiments that manipulate and operate pre-built biological networks. Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both efficient in parameters and attentive to time constraints.
We recognize current time representation approaches' shortcomings and suggest a
cycle-aware time-encoding framework for time characteristics that is universally
applicable and provides a more comprehensive time representation. Our unified
framework focuses on processing time-sensitive data within temporal knowledge graph
embeddings. Experimental results show that our proposed solutions equal or outperform
state-of-the-art models using semantic matching on multiple evaluation metrics. The
code for our research is available at https://github.com/hubofhub/Time-LowFER.

Within the RPA framework, the Jost function method has been enhanced to detect complex RPA eigenenergies in the complex energy plane. By applying this method, the RPA poles that characterize excited states such as $^{16}$O's electric dipole giant resonance were located within the complex energy plane with great success. Contrary to traditional views, research has revealed that the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance, which has historically been understood as a solitary and broad resonance, actually consists of multiple poles with distinct widths, origins, residual interaction responses, and distinct densities of fluctuation components within the RPA framework. Moreover, studies have found that the complexity of the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance, as identified by the Jost function method, is largely unaffected by the type of interaction used, suggesting that the multiple components that make up the resonance can coexist over a broad energy range due to the presence of a shape fluctuation plateau in this energy range. This finding is seen as having significant implications for the study of spectral functions in systems with multiple state coexistence within broad energy ranges.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest. In all cases, our algorithm showcases excellent performance in comparison to random walks and density-based clustering, as evaluated by clustering purity. This work is a starting point for further exploration of clustering in dynamic systems and raises significant research questions. The implementing code and data are available online at https://github.com/urivieira/cluster-dynamic-systems.

Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. The technique also enables improved performance on challenging datasets requiring significant stylistic changes. Our code is openly available at https://github.com/hjdw/SparseGAN.

Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at once.  This method results in enhanced precision when estimating population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters.  Notably, our study reveals that capture-recapture models alone can infer parameters for resource selection functions, enabling the exclusive use of capture data to investigate space usage, albeit with lower precision.  Nonetheless, using telemetry data yields superior precision.  We discovered that models employing standard encounter probability models can provide biased estimates of density when animals' spatial behavior correlates with environmental variables, which necessitates consideration of space usage in population density estimations through capture-recapture methods.  Our study utilized radio-telemetry and capture data from 227 radio-collared mountain lions (Puma concolor) in Colorado, USA, spanning nearly 20 years.  We believe that integrating capture-recapture and resource selection data offers a versatile framework for combining different data types and sources, thereby enhancing our capacity to investigate complex animal population and spatial ecology questions through a comprehensive approach.  This method is particularly useful for managing multiple components of the analysis and facilitating the inclusion of external environmental data, which can also be used for model selection and bayesian parameter estimation through markov chain monte carlo methods.  We outline a set of tools that can be employed to fit these models and conduct related analyses through our R package, spatialprocesscr, which is compatible with R and provides a user-friendly interface for capture-recapture models, including capture-recapture models, resource selection functions, and the combined space usage and resource selection models discussed in this study.  We intend this framework to serve as a platform for users to combine different capture-recapture models, resource selection functions, and spatial processes, as well as to facilitate the inclusion of external environmental data, and encourage users to explore other applications with us.  We provide a user-friendly tutorial that can be accessed through the R package

Notably, a k-approximation algorithm has been previously developed for this problem; however, whether such an algorithm exists with an approximation ratio sublinear in k even under the scenario of unit costs had yet to be determined. Moreover, we provide a $2k$-approximation algorithm for the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem under the scenario of unit costs. Evaluating defensive strategies in team sports can be complicated due to the limited availability of data from individual game events. Previous researchers developed methods for assessing football teams' defensive prowess by predicting the likelihood of gaining possession of the ball and being attacked, based on the location of all players involved. These earlier approaches, however, underestimated the importance of such events, assumed a perfect understanding of every player's position, and failed to account for diversity factors, such as player nationality and sex. To overcome these limitations, we present a revised approach to valuing defensive teams, by scaling the predicted probabilities of game events according to their scoring impact. By utilizing the publicly available player location data from broadcast videos of men's Euro 2020 and women's Euro 2022 football matches, we explored the effect of varying player numbers on prediction accuracy and validated our approach through an analysis of game data. The results showed that to accurately predict instances of being attacked, scoring, and conceding, it was sufficient to focus on all players involved, but ball gain predictions were most accurate with information on three to four key offensive and defensive players. Furthermore, our approach enabled us to provide insights into the superior defensive performances of finalist teams in the 2020 European Football Championship, and our methodology may also be applied to location data from other broadcast football matches. Additionally, we have made the data and code associated with our research publicly available, in the hope that it will contribute to a greater understanding of strategic variations in front of goal, and aid the development of more precise ball gain prediction models. This study's valuing approach and data release will serve as a platform for researchers to explore other aspects of football gameplay, such as the effectiveness of pressing and tackling, and provide valuable insights for coaches on improving game strategy. Ultimately, our approach represents an important step towards a more comprehensive analysis of football gameplay, and we are continuing to develop more sophisticated models that can be used in real-time with location data from broadcast videos, and we encourage coach and player feedback on these developments. Highly flexible recurrent state-space models can capture complex patterns in time series data, but typically assume a static and unchanging dynamic, a rare occurrence in real-world situations. To overcome this limitation, many systems exhibit patterns that are similar yet distinct, and can be described through a single underlying variable. To address this, we developed the Hidden Parameter Recurrent State Space Models (HiP-RSSMs), a novel framework that uses a compact set of latent factors to model interconnected dynamical systems. By implementing an efficient Gaussian graphical model, HiP-RSSMs can learn and conduct precise inference without resorting to approximations, such as variational inference. In our experiments, HiP-RSSMs consistently surpassed traditional state-space models and multi-task competitors on multiple demanding robotic tasks, in both real-world applications and simulations. The code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/master/hip_rssm.

We've established an additional consequence: almost sure asymptotic freeness of type $B$ for unitarily invariant random matrices. This consequence leads to several secondary findings: the asymptotic cyclic monotonicity, and the derivation of asymptotic conditional freeness. Specifically, we demonstrate the empirical spectral distribution of randomly rotated matrices converges towards a conditionally free convolution. This line of reasoning applies as well to an analysis of outlier eigenvalues in various unitarily invariant ensembles. Lastly, we discuss the scalability of these results to non-Hermitian matrices. We introduce HyperPrompt, an innovative architecture that utilizes HyperNetworks to create adaptable task-conditioning for self-attention in Transformers through prompt-based generation. In this setup, hyper-prompts can be optimized end-to-end by a HyperNetwork. By employing hyper-prompts as global task memories, HyperPrompt enables networks to learn task-specific features while facilitating flexible information sharing among multiple tasks. Notably, HyperPrompt offers a balance of high performance and efficient use of resources - it achieves exceptional performance with significantly fewer additional task-conditioning parameters compared to other methods, amounting to $0.14\%$ of the parameters required, ultimately showcasing great computational efficiency. Through thorough experimentation on diverse models and benchmarks, such as the GLUE and SuperGLUE tasks for Natural Language Understanding, HyperPrompt has consistently outperformed prominent multi-task learning approaches like Prompt-Tuning, HyperFormer++ and T5. The comprehensive evaluation includes a rigorous analysis of model performance along with an exploration of the effects of promoter length and network architecture. The code for HyperPrompt is openly available at https://github.com/chacza/HyperPrompt. Moreover, a paper detailing the findings has been submitted to IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. These characteristics make the algorithm versatile and effective across a wide spectrum of applications, including the distribution of degrees in sparse complex networks and the estimation of network size in scenarios of uncertainty. The algorithm has been thoroughly analyzed through a probabilistic approach and found to be robust against a substantial number of malicious nodes with the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. The algorithm has been evaluated through simulations on various types of complex networks, such as wireless sensor networks, where the number of malicious nodes approached the network size itself. The study demonstrated the algorithm's efficacy and reliability across a wide range of complex network scenarios. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. This breakthrough provides a substantial performance enhancement, enabling the computation of conformally flat spacetimes with 10-20 resolutions within a single day on a single processor. However, it also highlights the limitation that further developments are necessary to accommodate more intricate spacetimes and spacetimes with spin. Nonetheless, this method represents a crucial step forward for the evolution of inspirals in General Relativity. This work has been recognized by the 2021 award given to Andrew Hirschmann for outstanding work in numerical relativity. This paper has also inspired new lines of investigation, including the study of quasiperiodic solutions in higher dimensional spacetimes and the development of new methods for solving the Hamiltonian constraint through geometric and field theoretical approaches. This paper has raised significant questions regarding the existence of quasiperiodic solutions and the convergence of solutions found through iterative algorithms. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. Our results demonstrate notable enhancements in the anomalous Nernst effect and conductivity when considering the thermal stress and finite size effects, resulting in negative coefficients of approximately -0.15 W$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$. Notably, this study offers a framework for better understanding the anomalous Nernst effect in magnetic materials with intrinsically complex structures. Moreover, it highlights the potential for further research into the anomalous Nernst effect, and given its potential to generate large voltage outputs when combined with the anomalous Hall effect, it may also be suitable for the development of efficient thermal energy harvesting technologies. Understanding and identifying functional materials rely heavily on imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy. Recent advancements in automation and experimental techniques have significantly sped up and refined these measurements, producing copious amounts of data in need of analysis. These advancements are particularly pronounced at user facilities like synchrotron light sources. To process and interpret large datasets quickly, machine learning methods are continually being developed for real-time use in conjunction with measurements. Despite these developments, users without machine learning expertise often face significant barriers to integrating this technology into their experiments. To overcome these obstacles, this work presents several examples of machine learning models designed for real-time analysis across multiple beamlines at the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS-II), with a focus on incorporating them into existing workflows to enable easy integration into experiments. By leveraging this framework, users can easily combine machine learning models with their existing workflows via the Bluesky Suite for data management and experimental orchestration. As demonstrated with data across multiple user projects, this approach facilitates real-time data analysis to produce actionable results during the experiment, reducing data analysis times to near real-time. This work highlights several key applications, including crystal lattice determination, tomographic reconstruction, spectroscopic analysis, and 2D material characterization. By integrating machine learning into their experiments, users can expect faster analysis times, enhanced sensitivity, and the ability to investigate more complex phenomena. To facilitate widespread adoption, the developed models, workflows, and code are openly available on GitHub to empower the machine learning community to contribute their own models and modify the code for various applications. By doing so, this work aims to propel the integration of machine learning into user experiments at NSLS-II and beyond. A promising technique known as quantum annealing has been proposed for efficiently solving combinatorial optimization problems embedded in the Ising Hamiltonian's ground state. This approach involves two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian, whose gradual transformation from driver to problem form allows researchers to find the target ground state. Including non-stoquastic terms in the driver Hamiltonian is thought to enhance QA's performance, but a major challenge lies in decoherence hindering this process. Surprisingly, we demonstrate that including anti-ferromagnetic interactions within the Hamiltonian results in catastrophic QA failure even with infinitely long annealing periods, a consequence stemming from block-diagonalization and symmetry-related crossing during QA. Nevertheless, we find that adding a specific decoherence process can facilitate successful ground-state achievement for these problematic cases, a phenomenon attributed to environmental interference disrupting symmetry in quantum systems. This counterintuitive outcome yields profound insights into the fundamental workings of quantum annealing. Furthermore, our findings also offer potential new applications for studying the interplay between symmetry and decoherence in quantum systems. Moreover, we identify the threshold annealing time associated with these anti-ferromagnetic Hamiltonians, a threshold which can be exceeded by increasing the strength of decoherence. This counterintuitive outcome has significant implications for our understanding of quantum annealing and may lead to the development of new algorithms for studying the effects of symmetry in quantum systems subject to decoherence. This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory from 1921 to 1957, during the tenure of director Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who succeeded the lab's founder, Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn. When van Rhijn took over, the lab was working to implement Kapteyn's Selected Areas Plan. However, van Rhijn's contributions were marred by his lack of exploration into the broader implications of his findings, potentially stemming from limited creativity or vision. Throughout nearly his entire directorate, van Rhijn struggled to secure additional funding due to severe challenges including the 1930s Depression, the Second World War and its aftermath, his personal health issues during the 1940s, the lab's distant location, and a governmentally favored infrastructure in Leiden. Lastly, the circumstances that led to Adriaan Blaauw accepting the position of director in 1957, setting in motion the revitalization of the lab, are analyzed in the latter half of this study. The writing is informed by previously unexamined archival material, particularly the van Rhijn Archives held at the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory, although also drawing on established literature and additional sources. The evolution of the lab during this period was a story of survival against tremendous obstacles, followed by the catalysts necessary for renewal and growth. The implications of these findings are considered in the context of the lab's current status as a leading astronomical research center. The full development of the lab, its research, and its administration, remains, however, largely a story awaiting more comprehensive historical scrutiny. The current essay represents a initial foray into this topic, the results of which the editors have reviewed and approved. Focusing on the varying effects of remote learning on diverse demographic groups, data was collected from online learning modules in the Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters. Three indicators measured students' ability to stay on track: module submission rate, extra credit module submission rate, and engagement level with modules. Four demographic variables were analyzed - Gender, Ethnicity, Transfer Status, and First-generation status - and students were categorized into two groups based on each variable. Comparative analyses between each pair of demographic groups within the same semester, and between groups across semesters, were conducted to identify significant differences in student performance. In addition, exam and course scores in Fall 2020 were compared against those of the Fall 2019 semester, and against demographics groups. Findings showed that remote learning led to a decline in on-time and early module submission rates among first-generation students, but resulted in increased early submission rates among transfer students. Under-represented minority students demonstrated enhanced engagement with modules, while non-URM students exhibited similar levels of engagement before and during the pandemic. These outcomes highlight the varying effects of remote learning on students from different demographic backgrounds and underscore the importance of adaptable instructional designs that cater to the unique needs of a diverse higher-education student population. The study's findings can guide educators in refining their assessment and course design strategies to mitigate the negative effects of remote learning on first-generation students and ensure equitable learning experiences for all. The validity of this theory for near-extremal and extremal black holes is confirmed by analyzing their minimum function values after the scattering process. The findings show that neither near-extremal nor extremal black holes can become overcharged due to such processes. The outcome of scattering when a certain relationship between the electric potential and scalar field is met is that the extremal black hole retains its extreme properties. In contrast, when this relationship is not met, the scattering causes the extremal black hole to transform into a near-extremal black hole with a different mass and charge configuration. The outcome of scattering when this relationship is not met is that the near-extremal black hole breaks into two distinct objects: an extremal black hole and a particle with a mass and charge that corresponds to the difference in those parameters of the initial near-extremal black hole. The probability of determining one of these outcomes relies on the specific values of the mass and charge of the initial near-extremal black hole and the amount of energy exchanged during the scattering process. The extent to which this type of scattering can occur is determined by the horizon of the initial near-extremal black hole, as anything that exceeds this horizon cannot cause the black hole to become overcharged. Therefore, in this context, the horizon of the black hole effectively serves as a boundary that marks the start of the region over which its gravitational force wanes. Thus, in this scenario, the horizon of the black hole functions as a type of event horizon in the theoretical sense. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that in this scenario, the singularity within the event horizon of the black hole is concealed from view. Consequently, both the event horizon of the black hole and the singularity within it play a crucial role in defining the distinct properties of the extremal black hole. The extent to which the energy is transferred during the scattering process determines whether the extremal black hole will become overcharged, which is a highly significant finding. In this paper, we offer a groundbreaking reimagining of set theory through a
paracomplete and paraconsistent four-valued logic system. Unlike classical logic,
this approach accommodates propositions that may be neither entirely true nor
entirely false, as well as propositions that can simultaneously embody both
truths. We have devised a user-friendly axiomatic system, dubbed BZFC, by adapting
the ZFC-axioms to the parameters of a four-valued logic in a systematic manner.
Our key innovation involves the anti-classicality axiom, asserting the existence
of non-classical sets, with the unexpected outcome that the existence of a single
non-classical set allows for the generation of a wide array of non-classical sets.
Furthermore, our analysis encompasses the relationship between our proposed system
BZFC and classical ZFC, demonstrating that the two logics exhibit bidirectional
interpretability. We also demonstrate an interesting application concerning Tarski
semantics by showing how the traditional definition of the satisfaction relation
faithfully represents the non-classical properties inherent in our proposed meta-theory. 
Ultimately, our findings underscore the capability and versatility of set theory
implemented through a paracomplete and paraconsistent logic system.

Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. Ultimately, this work demonstrates the feasibility of using a non-invasive BCI approach with high resolution recordings to control the most complex aspect of gait, suggesting a bright future for this technology in the development of reliable lower limb prosthetics. This could not only improve the quality of life for individuals with spinal cord injuries but also offer a more secure and natural prosthetic walking experience for amputees. Conclusion: High-resolution cortical recordings can accurately decode walking state and step rate information from the motor cortices with high levels of precision, providing a strong basis for the development of reliable and safe lower limb prosthetics through biohybrid control. This work offers a promising future for this technology and suggests it has great potential to benefit both individuals with spinal cord injuries and lower limb amputees. This is achieved by developing a brain-computer interface that can safely and accurately control the complex aspects of gait, potentially leading to the creation of reliable and safe prosthetic devices for walking. This is done by training a machine learning algorithm on high-resolution recordings taken from the motor cortices of healthy individuals as they walk on a treadmill, providing an extremely precise level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information. Although the current study utilized a invasive recording method, the authors believe that similar results can be achieved with non-invasive methods such as EEG, offering a more user-friendly solution for this technology. Ultimately, this work demonstrates the potential for a brain-computer interface to safely and accurately control the most complex aspect of gait

This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness: one with a straightforward Gaussian distribution; another with a real-world experiment involving observation scheduling for signal period estimation; and a scenario with predicting future outcomes from past data under heavy-tailed conditions. Implementing this method in Python is also demonstrated. The results show that NS-based estimators can effectively compute uncertainty and relevance metrics even with a limited number of samples. However, they find that heavy-tailed data requires larger sample sizes to achieve accurate results. Consequently, we demonstrate that the Schreier graph of this component, relative to a base group generated by the actions on two adjacent vertices, is a connected component of the graph obtained by biacting on the tree. This result extends and refines previous findings by Bestvester and Fea for right-angled Artin groups whose action graphs have no triangles. Additionally, our results provide a new proof of a recent theorem by Bestvester and Fea. Furthermore, our paper explores the properties of right-angled Artin groups whose action graphs consist of a forest with a component that is a binary tree. The conjecture suggests that any right-angled Artin group with a non-trivial, minimal action on a tree that is not a line has an action graph without a binary component. To support this conjecture, we present the additional analysis of group actions on trees that are not lines, focusing on the scenario where the action graph contains a cycle. The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis has proven that NN meets three key conditions: it converges given the spectral norm condition is satisfied, achieves a convergence rate of one order higher for each additional inception depth, and has an optimal inception depth of one or two, subject to RAM constraints. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the NN applicable to massive sparse matrices at an increased computational cost, demonstrating its analytic equivalence to higher-order iterations. The Nested Neumann method can be used for matrix inversion in positive semi-definite matrices and general linear systems, including sparse, non-sparse, and complex matrices. In particular, we provide a new method for approximating matrix inversion in positive semi-definite matrices, based on NN, which leads to an innovative solution for the Poisson equation on a grid. We have also demonstrated the NN method's effectiveness through various numerical experiments. In addition, we present a new 'NN-Neumann' multi-right-hand-side extension of the algorithm, which enables efficient computation of multiple inversions by leveraging GPU-DirectX intercommunication. The Nested Neumann algorithm has numerous potential applications in scientific computation, data analysis, and machine learning. In our research, we have already achieved a 100x speedup for a particular Poisson equation computation, using a single NVIDIA V100 GPU, in comparison to classic direct inversion methods. The NN code has been openly shared for the community to explore and utilize its innovative algorithms. In the future, we plan to continue developing the NN algorithm, further accelerating its performance across multiple GPUs, exploring its integration with popular linear algebra libraries, and broadening its applicability to additional problem domains. These discrepancies stem from variations in network protocols used, leading to potential network noise and scalability limitations.
This study assesses the performance, scalability, and cost implications of running HPC applications on cloud infrastructure.

The findings also highlight the importance of accounting for cloud network characteristics in system design and model refinement.
Ultimately, the study suggests that cloud-based HPC deployments can provide performance comparable to that of on-premise systems, offering a viable alternative for conducting simulation-based research. Over time, the trend of companies adopting remote working has been on the rise, leading many to adapt Agile methodologies such as Scrum to cope with distributed teams. However, the global shift to fully remote working brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic was a unprecedented phenomenon. This research involves a two-phase, multi-method approach. Initially, it investigates how working from home affected Scrum practitioners through a qualitative survey. Subsequently, it proposes and empirically tests a theoretical framework using PLS-SEM with data from a sample of 200 software engineers who collaborated on Scrum projects from home. Our results demonstrate the reliability of all key constructs and the validity of all hypotheses, while also highlighting the advantages of combining home working and Scrum practices through an IPMA analysis. Notably, supporting employees' inherent needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness is crucial in the remote working context. Our findings indicate that both home working and Scrum use contribute to project success, with Scrum playing a mediating role. However, the analysis of interaction effects reveals that the Scrum method can mitigate the negative impact of home working on project success, suggesting that adopting Scrum from home requires consideration of its benefits and limitations. Our research provides actionable recommendations for project managers, IT leaders, and organizations seeking to manage distributed Scrum projects effectively. Lastly, our study offers directions for future research in this field. Despite the COVID-19 pandemic being the initial trigger for this research, its findings are relevant to the ongoing shift to remote working fueled by the pandemic. Additionally, our results are applicable to other Agile methodologies that share Scrum's fundamental characteristics. Ultimately, this study contributes to the evolution of Scrum in the home working context and paves the way for further research into the intersection of home working and Agile methods. This research has the potential to be replicated in the face of future significant changes that may alter the underlying variables in the studied context. This is exemplified by the COVID-19 pandemic's abrupt transition to a new normal, where researchers can investigate the long-term effects of this change and the associated consequences, as well as explore new research questions that emerge from the outcome. This is particularly relevant for the many companies that adopted Agile methodologies, including Scrum, in the pandemic era and are now reassessing their approaches in the post-pandemic era. This study aims to lay the groundwork for various replication studies that can be conducted in response to significant changes affecting the research context at hand. Events with the same level of centrality but varied average flow are used to investigate initial state conditions.  Results reveal that the event-shape selection's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient is unaffected by transverse momentum.  Also found is that charged hadron distributions are steeper for events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow, indicating interactions between radial and elliptic flow phenomena.  Utilizing hydrodynamic simulations with initial condition generators, predictions for event-shape selected outcomes are made and found to align with experimental data.  Radial and elliptic flow's connections are further explored by comparing results from different simulation models, revealing that events with elevated elliptic flow also exhibit increased radial flow.  This upsurge in radial flow is seen across various transverse momentum ranges.  Events with higher-than-average elliptic flow also exhibit increased charged hadron density, consistent with initial condition generator simulations.  This heightened charged hadron density's influence is mitigated, however, when considering transverse momentum distributions.  Events with higher-than-average elliptic flow were found to exhibit a greater contribution from radial flow, and for particles with higher transverse momentum.  This event-shape selection's connection to the initial state's geometry and temperature is explored, revealing that events with higher-than-average elliptic flow occur in regions with greater density, but also in areas where the initial condition's temperature plays a greater role.  This study expands the event-shape selected outcomes' understanding, unveiling details about the initial state's conditions and its relationships with radial and elliptic flow.  Additionally, this study highlights the importance of integrating data from various event-shape selected outcomes, ensuring that predictions align with a comprehensive range of outcomes, and incorporating possibilities for exploring connections with other experimental measurements.  Finally, this study's findings, derived from the 2.76 TeV collision energy, provide a solid foundation for further research in lower collision energies.  Also included in this study are results from 2.76 TeV collisions but with a broader centrality range, as well as results from 5.02 TeV collisions with a more refined centrality range. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Therefore, our multiple-time-step algorithm provides a significant improvement for accurate simulations of complex sediment transport by incorporating particle collisions. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. Ultimately, the robot reached 70% of the desired height in a single hop. However, larger foot sizes resulted in decreased efficiency due to the buildup of granular material beneath the foot. To move forward, we propose integrating this ground reaction force model into a state estimation and control framework for multi-legged robots. This approach has the potential to enable these robots to adapt to varying ground conditions, such as the addition of foreign objects to the terrain, and ensure stable and efficient movement. To achieve this, additional research is necessary to enhance the RFT-based model's predictive capabilities. This could be done by introducing an empirical parameter to the RFT model or developing a more sophisticated model that accounts for the distribution of ground grains. This work has the potential to contribute to the development of more efficient and adaptive control systems for multi-legged robots navigating deformable terrain. Although previous research has thoroughly analyzed the complex interactions of a liquid droplet under an electrical influence in air, the droplet's effects on the surrounding gas phase have been underrepresented. A notable phenomenon arises when the droplet undergoes significant oscillations, induced by the presence of a resonating electric field. The air circulation patterns that emerge as a result create localized aerodynamic forces that impede the droplet's ability to attract particulate matter in its vicinity, especially when the droplet is immersed in an aerosol cloud. The interplay between the droplet and its surroundings sparks curiosity in scientists, who see the potential for further discoveries in this two-phase system, encompassing both gas and liquid components, especially with regards to the transport of heat and mass. Furthermore, the droplet's oscillatory behavior could be tailored to modify the surrounding air's physical properties, thus potentially enriching the physics involved. The current study focuses on exploring the droplet's impact on the transportation of particulate matter in the airborne phase by examining the droplet's oscillatory motion and resulting aerodynamic forces as it interacts with the surrounding air and is affected by the presence of the electric field. The droplet's response to the electrical stimulation is described by a modified version of the Reynolds equation, which is solved numerically to derive the droplet's shape and the resulting circulating air patterns. The introduced circulation theory is then utilized to assess the droplet's influence on the transportation of particulate matter in the airborne phase. The presented investigation highlights the droplet's oscillatory motion and the resulting air circulation patterns, along with the associated aerosol dynamic forces, and reveals the droplet's capacity to modulate the transport of particulate matter in its vicinity. The study demonstrates that the droplet's ability to attract particulate matter is significantly impeded due to the air circulation patterns induced by the oscillations, especially when the droplet is immersed in an aerosol cloud. Effective communication through language cannot be fully achieved without considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, even the best-performing model (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) managed only 42% accuracy according to our consistency metric, significantly lagging behind the 81% achieved by human evaluators. In a bid to fuel further NLP innovations, we publicly release our dataset, along with comprehensive evaluations involving fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot scenarios. Our research underscores the significance of advanced NLP models being able to accurately process negation without relying on simplistic theories and anticipates significant breakthroughs in this domain. As such, we encourage researchers to tackle this challenging problem and share their results on our publicly available evaluation dataset. It is available at this link: https://github.com/ghrua/Condaqa. It has also been incorporated into the Leaderboard of the ACL Findings 2022, along with other notable NLP datasets. It is worth noting that our work distinguishes itself from existing studies processing negation via NLP models. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. The results presented further highlight the practical value of studying quantum quench in the context of quantum annealing, offering a path toward developing more effective quantum annealing algorithms. $d$ and $s$ orbital types for infinite layered nickelates, we investigate the
extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to a mixture of filled and weakly
coupled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands and results in self-doped $d$ orbital and
$d$-wave pairing tendencies emerging. 
Interestingly, strong screening allows for another one-band physics approximation,
this time incorporating significant weight transfer when an extra filled $s$-band
is included, exhibiting both one-band physics and Kondo-lattice-like behavior,
which arises solely from this single model. 
Includes discussions on both the limitations of such one-band models in relation
to experimentally obtained spectra and the possible exits from the highly
insulating, $d$-wave ground state through other one-band or multi-band scenarios. 
Also includes a discussion on possible connections to experimentally obtained
data.

By analyzing initial conditions with sufficiently small magnitudes regardless of the collision rate, the study reveals various dynamic processes arising from the combination of the phase-mixing/dispersive effects of the transport operator and the singular collision operator. In regions where high-frequency fluctuations are prevalent, an accelerated decay phenomenon is observed, characterized by an exponential decrease in a time scale that inversely correlates with the collision rate and the frequency magnitude. In contrast, for regions where fluctuations are minimal, Taylor dispersion leads to an accelerated decay governed by the inverse of the frequency squared, multiplied by the collision rate. Moreover, this research proves the existence of almost uniform phase mixing estimates. We use radiance data from space to study wave slopes in oceans during the day, specifically using about 300 channels between 3.6 and 4.0 $\mu$m, which takes into account solar radiation reflected off the water. This approach uses a large dataset of around 150 million observations, enabling the derivation of wind-speed dependent wave-slope probabilities up to 15 m/s. Our method reevaluates Cox and Munk's methodology for determining wave-slope probability distribution from photographs of sun glints, offering an alternative, more robust approach for retrieving parameters of a probability distribution function. Our results for wave slope statistics are comparable to previous findings, yet our data exhibits reduced uncertainties that pinpoint potential discrepancies between observed wave behaviors and previous models at moderate wind speeds. Our study also highlights how wave slope statistics change as wind speed increases, specifically noting the impact on skewness, kurtosis coefficients, and the behavior of updown wind asymmetry. Notably, our results indicate that waves become more positively skewed and exhibit greater kurtosis as wind speed increases, which aligns with the expectations of models that describe wave growth. Conversely, our data reveals negligible changes in the quadrupole moment of wave slopes despite varying wind conditions, which may indicate that the distribution of wave energies holds a constant shape despite increasing wind forces. Ultimately, our research provides a theoretical framework that could inform models of wave behavior, which in turn would improve their ability to predict sea states when coupled with dynamical core models in global numerical weather prediction systems. Nonetheless, further research is needed to fully incorporate these findings into operational use. unintentionally impact other parts, hindering overall system performance. This is
addressed by conducting regression testing, which re-evaluates system sections
aimed at preventing adverse effects. However, pinpointing these affected areas
proves challenging, making it essential to identify system changes through a
different approach. We apply singular value decomposition to group software
modifications by their functional roles, allowing for more efficient detection
of areas requiring retesting during subsequent updates. By leveraging parallel
calculations on shared memory systems, we enhance testing speed, ensuring optimal
results can be obtained even as software systems scale up. Concurrent testing
also enables continuous integration and continuous deployment methods. Experimental
results using the Linux kernel as a test subject show significant gains in testing
speed and efficiency. Overall, our method provides a data-driven approach for
optimal regression testing. The testing accelerator, along with relevant code,

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread disruption, with numerous countries enforcing strict lockdowns and millions of lives affected. In an effort to cope with the emotional impact, people are increasingly expressing their sentiments on social networks, utilizing microblogging platforms as a means of seeking comfort. Twitter has emerged as a prime platform for exchanging ideas, with users posting diverse sentiments aimed at promoting awareness about staying home and maintaining social distancing. However, there is a growing concern regarding the dissemination of fake news that aims to frighten people, emphasizing the need to differentiate between positive, negative, and neutral thoughts to effectively disseminate beneficial opinions to a wider audience. Consequently, identifying and interpreting the context of large datasets on Twitter has become a significant challenge. In this paper, a comprehensive analysis of Twitter data using various machine learning algorithms was conducted to evaluate sentiment, and subsequent context learning of the dataset based on sentiment was explored. Our research employed Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machines, and Logistic Regression algorithms to analyze the context of the dataset, and the results revealed that the LGNN algorithm exhibited superior performance in context learning. Moreover, context-aware classification was carried out using the trained models, and our research demonstrated the benefits of context learning over batch performance. Our research provides novel insights into context learning and can serve as a foundation for further investigations in this area. All source code and datasets used in this paper are available for reference at https://github.com/rahuljha001/Context-Aware-Twitter-Dataset. Furthermore, the paper has been presented at the 10th International Conference on Advanced Data and Information Analysis, held in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, from December 19 to 21, 2021.

Initially, the Lawrence-Doniach and interlayer tunneling models were the prominent theoretical concepts to describe cuprate superconductors by connecting CuO planes through Josephson coupling. Yet, the discovery of larger than predicted interlayer magnetic penetration depths in these materials raised issues with the tunneling model's validity. The emergence of planar stripes and charge domains enabled alternative Josephson coupling theories. Our study finds the average intralayer interaction to be greater than interlayer coupling and comparable to condensation energy, ultimately yielding long-range phase order-driven superconductivity. As an outcome, the relationship between the square of interlayer and intralayer penetration depths to the respective resistivity ratios exhibits proportionality near the superconducting transition, corroborated by multiple measurements. The ratio of the longest Josephson coupling length to penetration depth defines the phase domain size, calculated to be in the range of 10 to 100 units of lattice parameter, depending on the material, thus providing a long sought-after length scale for the superconducting state. The predicted proportionality and length scale are applicable to all optimized cuprate superconductors. Ultimately, our findings validate the efficacy of the London theory in describing cuprate superconductors and offer a new perspective on the physics governing these materials. The proposed approach is proposed as a model to be tested by researchers in the cuprate superconductivity community. The suggested plan involves simulating temperature-dependent phase diagrams of various cuprate superconductors using the proposed Josephson coupling architecture, with the goal of comparing the results to experimental data. The delivered dataset will serve as a base for further theoretical modeling and experimental validation, enabling the development of more intricate theories for cuprate superconductivity. The Josephson architecture, temperature-dependent phase diagrams, phase domain size, and the ratio of the longest Josephson coupling length to penetration depth are the key deliverables from this study. The findings can be expanded to encompass other materials with layered Josephson coupling, such as strontium titanate and barium strontium titanate, providing opportunities for further theoretical and experimental investigation. The proposed approach provides a long-term framework for the cuprate superconductivity research community, enabling the development of more intricate theories for superconductivity in these materials. The approach can be expanded to encompass other materials with layered Josephson coupling, such as strontium titanate and barium strontium titanate, providing opportunities for further theoretical and experimental investigation. The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index within neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars.  By simulating the hadron-quark phase transition with different interface tension, we found the sound velocity's expected behavior could also arise from the quark phase's nonperturbative properties.  Consequently, this could result in a denser star with similar mass, thus providing the groundwork for a new type of quark star equation of states that may be tested through high-precision pulsar radius measurements.  Our findings demonstrate that the relationship between sound velocity and density can serve as an identifiable quark star feature. An anti Tai mapping, defined as the subset $M$ of $V_1\times V_2$, excludes any node pairs $(x,y)$ and $(x',y')$ that would conflict with each other's ancestral hierarchy, given that $x<x'$ indicates $x$ is an ancestor of $x'$. High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach assesses hypothetical distortions in general relativity's influence on astronomical observations. A key factor influencing these measurements is a post-Newtonian parameter, denoted by $\gamma$, which measures the gravitational impact on light deflection. Analyzing this parameter, we studied the effects of varying $\gamma$ on parallax measurements from a mission like Gaia, both mathematically and computationally. Analytical calculations of variable PPN $\gamma$'s effect on observables revealed that a change in this parameter causes a global shift in parallax measurements. This led us to develop a formula linking this shift to the satellite's position, the angle between its axis and the direction to the Sun, and the uncertainty of PPN $\gamma$. Computational simulations validated our theoretical predictions. We have developed an efficient approach for condensing complex systems into their fundamental behaviors using their primary underlying features. By leveraging observed data, we pinpoint a low-dimensional structure that characterizes the systems' gradual evolution and generate an extremely simple representation of the systems' dynamics within that structure. Building on the SSMLearn algorithm, which applies implicit optimization to fit a system's underlying structure to available data and simplifies the systems' dynamics, we have created two more direct methods that transform the process into explicit problems under specific assumptions. These algorithms demonstrate the ability to create precise and highly simplified models for complex systems on both numerical and real-world datasets, significantly reducing the computational time. Moreover, our results validate the feasibility of our methods in providing a system's underlying features and dynamics using only limited observed data. Our work provides a critical step towards developing data-driven methods for analyzing complex systems by providing a feasible solution to the condensation problem. Our algorithms and related code are openly accessible, offering a valuable tool for condensing complex systems and facilitating further research in this area.

This concise analysis presents a pair of two-component Bose-Einstein condensate models which can accurately predict the existence of self-accelerating solitons. One such model, featuring interacting 1D solitons, involves a binary BEC trapped within an optical-lattice potential and utilizes interaction forces with opposite signs to create an equilibrium where both solitons accelerate equally. Meanwhile, the total momentum remains conserved. Another model, derived from Gross-Pitaevskii equations for resonantly-coupled atomic components using a microwave field, facilitates an exact transformation to a moving frame of reference, thus providing predictions for one- and two-dimensional stable self-accelerating solitons, including vortex rings. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server.
